#2525. Josh Downs trade grades: Chiefs, Patrick Mahomes get help, Colts get value for disgruntled WR

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Everyone got what they wanted in the Josh Downs trade. Downs, who demanded a trade earlier this season, got his wish just before the 2026 NFL trade deadline buzzer Tuesday afternoon. The Indianapolis Colts sent him, along with a 2027 seventh-round pick (via the Buffalo Bills), to the Kansas City Chiefs in exchange for a 2027 fourth-round pick and a 2027 fifth-round pick.

Downs now goes from catching passes from Daniel Jones, whose 82.3 passer rating ranks 34th out of 35 qualified quarterbacks this season, to catching passes from Patrick Mahomes, a three-time Super Bowl MVP. That's why he tweeted the gif of Vince Carter expressing gratitude in reaction to the news that he is now a Chief.

He quickly followed up that post by tweeting, "I am beyond grateful and blessed for my time in Indy. Nothing but love for the [horse] Shoe."

So how did the Colts and Chiefs make out in this trade deadline deal? Here is a look at the grade for each squad.

The Chiefs (6-2) are always in win-now mode, with Mahomes (31 years old), tight end Travis Kelce (37), defensive tackle Chris Jones (32), defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo (66) and head coach Andy Reid (68) getting up there in age. Kelce, Rashee Rice, who is coming back from an offseason knee surgery, and former first-round pick Xavier Worthy haven't been getting the job done.

Kansas City is averaging 117.5 receiving yards per game by wide receivers this season, which is the fewest of the Mahomes era (since 2018) and ranks 28th in the NFL this season. That's why the Chiefs went out and traded for Downs.

The 25-year-old Downs has been a weapon out of the slot since entering the league as a third-round pick in 2023: His 1,995 yards receiving out of the slot are the second most in the entire NFL in the span of his career, trailing only Detroit Lions All-Pro wide receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown (2,160).

* Downs was drafted in the third round of the 2023 NFL Draft

Sure, Downs is a rental playing out the final year of his rookie contract in 2026, but Kansas City was desperate. Plus, if Downs builds a nice rapport with Mahomes, this deal could lead to a second contract come the 2027 offseason. It's also a huge win that the Chiefs didn't have to part with any Day 2 draft capital.

Downs requested a trade, and he is playing out the final year of his rookie contract. There was no chance he would be open to re-signing with Indianapolis in the 2027 offseason, especially with the Colts set to dive headfirst into a rebuild with a new general manager. The Colts did well to get multiple early Day 3 draft picks for a disgruntled player who already had one foot out the door.

#2524. Re-grading the Jaylen Brown-Paul George trade: Celtics' grade has greatly improved, 76ers' mark stays perfect

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Besides the Luka Dončić stunner, you could argue that this summer's Jaylen Brown blockbuster was the most surprising trade in recent NBA history. A former Finals MVP coming off of his best season traded for ... Paul George? Someone widely treated as one of the NBA's worst contracts and half of the draft capital a superstar typically fetches? The reactions were, obviously, extreme. Celtics fans revolted. Pundits expected a meaningful drop-off for Boston. Trade graders like myself pilloried Brad Stevens and his front office for moving a 29-year-old All-NBA forward for what appeared to be far less than fair value.

And yet, as Brown prepares to face his former employer for the first time, the two teams sit neck-and-neck in the Eastern Conference. The 76ers top the standings at 9-2. The Celtics are right behind them at 8-2, but have the East's best net rating at +11.6. While Philadelphia has thus far gotten exactly what it wanted out of the trade, the Celtics seemingly have as well. So with their first of potentially many high-stakes clashes this season set for Tuesday night (8 p.m. ET, NBC/fubo), let's revisit the trade and hand out revised grades for the offseason's most impactful trade.

The backlash to the George-for-Brown trade was fundamentally centered on two premises:

The first premise was, frankly, outdated in the apron era. Yes, Kevin Durant netted four first-round picks, a first-round swap, and players who would go on to net six additional first-round picks and another swap, but that was all the way back in February 2023, and that trade completely derailed Phoenix's future. The James Harden trade played out similarly for the Nets. Teams are more skittish about all-in moves for older players than they've ever been.

There have been outlier, extremely high-cost trades since then, but all came under somewhat irreplicable circumstances. Mikal Bridges netted five first-round picks and a swap, for instance, but he never misses games, came with two years of cheap cost-control and played collegiately with several other key Knicks. New York viewed him as the finishing piece of a championship team, and the Knicks were ultimately proven correct.

Desmond Bane wasn't as underpaid, but he fit the extremely narrow niche the Magic needed: someone who could enhance their offense without commanding high usage on a team that was already locked into two max-salary shot-creators or compromising their defensive identity. There were maybe a handful of players in the NBA Orlando could have targeted for that role, and Bane, amazingly, was probably the only one available. In an extremely injured Eastern Conference, the Magic tried to be opportunistic. That's where these lopsided trades happen. They're almost always circumstantial.

The more typical star trade scenario is something closer to what the Milwaukee Bucks went through with Giannis Antetokounmpo. The player is older, attempts to fix things internally have failed, and the relationship between star and team is no longer tenable. The acquiring team typically has a leverage advantage, and that's especially true in the apron era, where paying the sort of giant salaries these stars get in their early 30s carries far more risk than reward. Antetokounmpo netted three picks, one swap and a handful of players that won't be foundational for the Bucks. We know Antetokounmpo had more trade value than Brown because the Celtics tried to trade Brown and more for Antetokounmpo, but a deal wasn't struck. So if Antetokounmpo, a two-time MVP, was worth three-and-a-half picks plus some player value, Brown being worth two picks and some player value feels in line with the new, cost-conscious NBA.

And then of course, there's the matter of what the player value actually was. That brings us to George. From November through January of last season, George averaged just 16 points on 42-38-86 shooting. This was in line with his 2024-25 performance, and together, the year-and-a-half sample felt reliable for an aging star. Well, George then got suspended 25 games. When he returned in March, he was a 21-point scorer on better shooting splits who looked rejuvenated defensively. He went on to torch the Celtics in the first round of the playoffs. Most of us expected George to look more like the player he was before that suspension in Boston. The Celtics bet that he would look like who he was after, and thus far, they've looked correct.

The raw numbers are superb: 20.4 points, 47-43-81 shooting and his highest assist and rebounding rates since he left the Clippers. The fit has been even better. Much was made of how low many advanced metrics are on Brown relative to his reputation, but the more significant story here was always his outlier status within Boston's intended team structure. Joe Mazzulla wants to maximize 3-point attempt rate. George's 3-point attempt rate so far this season (51.4%) is nearly twice Brown's (27.8%). Brad Stevens spoke openly about not wanting to concentrate usage in two players, and George's usage rate is nearly eight percentage points lower than Brown's was a year ago. The Celtics wanted this sort of player in their system and next to Jayson Tatum, and it's working.

Yet just as vitally, George is helping the Celtics diversify a bit as a team. The Celtics generated the second-fewest turnovers in the NBA last season. They're averaging the eighth-most in the NBA thus far this season, and George is the single biggest reason why. Only Dyson Daniels and Scottie Barnes are averaging more deflections, and among players who have played at least four games, only Daniels and Kris Dunn are generating more steals.

The Celtics had the lowest free-throw attempt rate in the NBA last season as well. They're right around the middle of the pack this year. Tatum is the one drawing most of those fouls, but George is a critical part of the structure that gets Tatum to the line. Brown can be a bit of a ball-stopper. Among true forwards, only Kawhi Leonard and Zion Williamson averaged more seconds per touch than Brown a year ago. The average George touch this season lasts 3.3 seconds compared to just under five for Brown a year ago. It's simply easier to compromise a defense when the ball is moving and players are making quick decisions. That's how defenses are forced into rotation and wind up fouling out of desperation. As a team, the Celtics have the sixth-lowest average time per touch this season compared to the eighth-highest a year ago.

Even the contract feels a bit more palatable now than it did at the time. Brown would have become eligible for an extension on his supermax contract last offseason, and based on the season he had, he would have been more than justified in asking for one. The Celtics, clearly, had no plans to commit extra years to Brown on top of the three that he was already owed. George isn't quite living up to his supermax price tag thus far this season, but his deal is a year shorter and comes with no such extension pressure.

If anything, his player option for next season opens some interesting doors for the Celtics if they decide they're happy with this partnership. As of right now, the Celtics have around $3 million in first-apron room for the 2027-28 season based on current projections. Say they want to use the full mid-level exception on a free agent or perhaps need a bit more wiggle room to make a trade. They could theoretically go to George and ask him to lower his cap figure in exchange for another year of security. Turning a one-year, $56.6 million deal into, say, a two-year, $90 million deal could make sense for both sides provided George sustains this level of play.

The reasonable fear that he might not is why we stop at a "B-" for Boston. This is still his age-36 season. George has been injury-prone for most of his career. He presumably will not get a 25-game break this season, and even if he's this good all year, all of these benefits he's brought to Boston are somewhat regular-season-centric. The playoffs are a different game, one that leans much more into Brown's strengths as an individual shotmaker and man-to-man defender. The Celtics still never get to the rim. Their best answer for opposing star guards is probably Jordan Walsh, whose offense makes him hard to play for too long. If Boston flames out in the playoffs, we might view Brown's absence as one of the bigger reasons why. The path to actually winning this trade gets paved in April and May.

But for now, at least, it's starting to make sense. The Celtics added two premium draft assets in a way that allowed them to maintain their existing playing style and avoid taking a major step back in the present. They sidestepped what probably would have been an ugly contract negotiation, and the more barbs get traded in the press, the clearer it becomes that this situation simply was not salvageable. The Celtics had to trade Brown. The offers were far lower than we anticipated. Boston still managed to make the best of less-than-ideal circumstances and still factors prominently into the Eastern Conference championship picture.

Funnily enough, you could pretty easily argue that George would actually be a far better fit for this iteration of the 76ers than Brown is. Philadelphia's 20th-ranked offense has a bottom-five 3-point attempt rate and the eighth-highest average seconds per touch in the NBA. The Sixers could stand to trade some of that dribbling for a bit more shooting. Considering how lethal their transition offense can be, George's turnover generation would also fit this defense like a glove. The 76ers will get better offensively. We're still in tiny-sample season, and everyone's still learning how to play together. But George is undeniably the easier player to fit onto a roster like this than Brown.

Of course, the 76ers wouldn't have a roster like this without Brown. Widespread reporting has made it clear that Philadelphia's acquisition of Brown was what first caught the attention of LeBron James in free agency. If Brown was indeed a swing factor in the 76ers getting LeBron, that assuages any short-term salary concerns for Brown. For God's sake, the Philadelphia 76ers have LeBron James on a minimum contract. Even if Brown is overpaid, the surplus value on the James contract more than offsets any negative value there.

The 76ers have far less reason to fear an extension than Boston did as well. By trading Brown, the Celtics subjected him to the NBA's six-month extend-and-trade restrictions. That meant he could only tack one year onto his contract rather than two, and because he has multiple years remaining on his contract, he's not eligible to extend during the season. The 76ers therefore get to table those discussions until the offseason at the earliest, and remember, at that point, Brown will be negotiating off of the more modest statistics that come with sacrificing for the sake of a superteam. It's simply easier to envision Brown extending at less than the max in Philadelphia than it would have been in Boston.

Speaking of sacrificing, remember the whole "Jaylen Brown wants his own team" narrative from last offseason? For all we know, it was true at the time and might have remained true had he stayed with the Celtics. So far, that has been a complete non-issue for the 76ers. Brown is currently sporting his lowest usage rate since 2020 (before he became an All-Star). He's turning the ball over around half as often per 100 possessions as he did a season ago. He's an enormous part of a defense that surprisingly ranks No. 6 in the NBA so far this season. He's even openly called the 76ers Tyrese Maxey's team.

And the 76ers are, obviously, winning. They're mostly winning clutch games, but hey, you expect to win close games with four stars in your starting lineup. They're going to figure out the finer points of maximizing this talent mix over time, but even the "getting to know each other" version of this group poses almost impossible matchup problems for other teams. Take Cleveland, who has already faced Philadelphia twice. Can you guess which two Cavalier defenders have spent the most partial possessions guarding Brown, per NBA.com tracking data? James Harden and Donovan Mitchell, at 60.6 combined. Those are the sort of defenders you try to hide on weak scorers to preserve for offense. Well, where exactly are Harden and Mitchell supposed to hide against this team? There are no weak spots. The advantage of having this many creators is that Philadelphia basically starts every possession with an exploitable mismatch.

On pure talent accumulation alone, this is the sort of roster teams tend to go all-in for. Philadelphia didn't even have to. While the Stepien Rule complicates the tradability of some of their remaining picks, the 76ers are still slated to have four first-round picks in the next seven drafts. There is still ammunition for some sort of pivot here, whether that's a short-term upgrade to maximize this title run or more likely, some sort of long-term change at center as Joel Embiid gets older and potentially less reliable from a health perspective.

There are going to be depth questions down the line. Even if Brown gets less than a 35% max on his eventual extension, he's going to be pricey. Maxey feels like a near-lock for a supermax extension in the years to come, and while VJ Edgecombe will almost certainly be limited to 25% of the cap on his rookie extension, he'll still account for quite a bit of money. The 76ers are a top-heavy roster today, and that's after hitting a few home runs on the margins and getting arguably the greatest player of all time to take the minimum. Sustaining contention beyond the "Embiid is still a matchup nightmare and LeBron is on the team" era is going to require near-perfect management on the margins.

But this isn't rocket science. How many teams have a trio they can feel better about for, say, the next three-to-five years than Maxey, Brown and Edgecombe? The Brown trade opened an immediate championship window and likely ensured a relatively high baseline for the rest of the decade, assuming acceptable health and wise decisions elsewhere on the roster. It was a great trade in July and it remains a great trade today.

#2523. 2026 MLB Manager of the Year: White Sox's Will Venable, Brewers' Pat Murphy win BBWAA awards

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Chicago White Sox manager Will Venable and Brewers manager Pat Murphy were named the Managers of the Year in their respective leagues on Tuesday night as part of the BBWAA's awards week. Murphy is the first manager to ever win the award in three consecutive seasons.

The annual awards, which also include Manager of the Year, Reliever of the Year, Cy Young and MVP, are voted on by 30 members of the Baseball Writers Association of America (that's two per MLB city in each league). Votes were submitted before the beginning of the playoffs, meaning that only regular-season contributions are taken into account.

Murphy, manager of the World Series champion Milwaukee Brewers, has been voted the National League Manager of the Year, the Baseball Writers Association of America announced on Tuesday. He is the first person to win three consecutive Manager of the Year awards and the tenth person with three Manager of the Year wins in total.

Ballots for the BBWAA's awards are submitted between the end of the regular season and the beginning of the postseason. They are regular-season awards and Milwaukee's World Series win did not factor into the voting.

Of course, Murphy did not need the World Series win to boost his Manager of the Year case. He guided the small-market Brewers to baseball's best record (103-59) and run differential (+214) during the regular season, and their fourth consecutive NL Central title. Their 103 wins are a franchise record and baseball's most since 2023.

Murphy just completed his third season as Brewers manager and has three Manager of the Year wins to show for it. Bobby Cox (2004-05), Kevin Cash (2020-21), and Stephen Vogt (2024-25) are the only others with two consecutive Manager of the Year awards. Vogt was not an American League Manager of the Year finalist this season.

Prior to Murphy's threepeat here, the Brewers had never had a Manager of the Year winner. He's won the award now three times in three years at the helm.

Atlanta Braves manager Walt Weiss and Philadelphia Phillies manager Don Mattingly finished behind Murphy in the voting. Mattingly took over as an interim after the Phillies fired Rob Thomson on April 28. Philadelphia had baseball's fourth-best record after the managerial change. Weiss guided the Braves to the NL East title.

Venable, who helped orchestrate a 24-win year-to-year improvement and guided the team to its first postseason berth since 2021, has been named the American League Manager of the Year, the Baseball Writers Association of America announced on Tuesday. He beat out Tampa Bay Rays manager Kevin Cash and Boston Red Sox manager Chad Tracy.

The White Sox went 84-78 in 2026 after going 60-102 in 2025 and a hideous 41-121 in 2024. Those 121 losses are the record in baseball's Modern Era (since 1900). Venable's White Sox are the first team in history to reach the postseason after losing at least 100 games in the previous two seasons (they also lost 101 games in 2023).

The huge steps forward seem to be what secured the award for Venable. He took over in 2025 and the White Sox improved by 19 wins that season, only to turn around and improve by 24 more wins this past season. They were arguably the most surprising playoff team in 2026 and Venable gets his due here.

Venable joins the following White Sox manager of the year winners:

Cash finishes as the runner-up in a very close vote. Venable got 15 of the 30 first-place votes while Cash got 12. Tracy finishes in third place, with Guardians manager Stephen Vogt fourth and Yankees' skipper Aaron Boone sitting fifth.

Cash's Rays improved by 21 games to win an AL-best 98 and win the AL East after finishing in fourth place in 2025. Tracy took over the Red Sox after Alex Cora started 10-17 and was fired. Tracy went 77-58 and earned the second AL wild card.

#2522. Fernando Mendoza inherits a 4-5 Raiders team and NFL history offers two wildly different outcomes

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

In 2016, the Rams were 4-5 when they benched Case Keenum and handed the offense to No. 1 overall pick Jared Goff. He lost all seven of his starts, threw five touchdowns and seven interceptions, and LA finished 4-12. Jeff Fisher was fired with three games remaining, the Rams hired Sean McVay that offseason, and the rest is history.

Two years later, the Ravens were also 4-5 when Lamar Jackson, the final pick of the first round in 2018, replaced an injured Joe Flacco. He won six of his first seven starts, and Baltimore won the AFC North before losing to the Chargers in the wild-card round. Jackson threw just five touchdowns, but his ability to run transformed everything about the offense.

Same record. Same point in the season. Two completely different outcomes.

And now comes Fernando Mendoza, the No. 1 pick in April's draft, who inherits a 4-5 Raiders team after Las Vegas traded Kirk Cousins to Minnesota on Tuesday for a third-round pick. Mendoza will make his first start Sunday against the Seahawks, and while it's tempting to think nine weeks on the bench may have helped prepare him for what's next, history suggests it could be a little more complicated than that.

Since 2000, 148 quarterbacks have started at least one game as NFL rookies. Just 22 made their first start between Weeks 10 and 13, and their collective debuts were not pretty.

They completed just 53.8% of their passes, averaged 5.8 yards per attempt and threw interceptions on 5.3% of their dropbacks – the worst marks of any group. Only five of those 22 won their debuts, and their interception rate was more than 1.6 times that of rookies who started in Week 1.

How rookie QBs performed in their first career start, 2000-2025

Of course, circumstances matter. Some quarterbacks sat because they weren't ready. Others played because the starter got hurt or was ineffective. But the takeaway remains: Sitting for half a season doesn't guarantee a smoother transition to the top of the depth chart.

Five teams had winning records when they turned to a rookie in Weeks 10-13. They were a combined 30-19 before the change and went 10-20 afterward. The 17 teams with losing records fared slightly better when they installed a rookie under center, improving their winning percentage from 28.9% to 33.7% – though they still lost twice as often as they won.

Team performance before and after a rookie's first start, Weeks 10-13

Only three of those 22 teams made the playoffs. The 2011 Texans turned to T.J. Yates after injuries to Matt Schaub and Matt Leinart. The 2017 Bills benched Tyrod Taylor for Nathan Peterman despite sitting at 5-4. Peterman threw five interceptions in the first half of his debut, Taylor reclaimed the job at halftime, and Buffalo eventually made the playoffs with Taylor back under center.

Jackson was different. Baltimore initially needed him because Flacco was injured, but he played so well that they stuck with him even after Flacco was healthy. Obviously, that's a blueprint the Raiders would love to follow, but it's fair to say the organizational infrastructure isn't quite there yet.

And then there are the more immediate concerns for the Raiders rookie…

Mendoza's first three starts come against Seattle, Denver and Cleveland, which also happen to be three of the league's best defenses. The schedule gets less daunting after a Week 13 bye, though matchups against the Broncos and Chiefs make up two of the Raiders; final four games. So yeah.

There is a bigger issue: Mendoza could play well and still lose a bunch of games, and Vegas' first nine weeks help explain why.

Kirk Cousins wasn't the reason for all the losing when Vegas traded him. He had thrown 20 touchdowns and just eight interceptions, and the team was averaging 25.4 points per game. Their passing offense ranks fifth in yards per game and ninth in EPA per play, so Mendoza isn't walking into a no-win situation.

The problems lie everywhere else. Las Vegas ranks dead last in yards per carry (2.9), 31st in rushing yards per game (71.3) and 30th in rushing success rate. The defense hasn't been much better, allowing 35.7 points per game over the last six weeks, five of them losses.

That's a tough combination for any quarterback, future Hall of Famer or fresh face of the franchise. Kubiak's system can help, but even the best-designed offense needs a run game that provides some balance.

Back in June, I wrote that Mendoza might be the most NFL-ready quarterback in the class but had landed in the least quarterback-friendly situation. My rookie QB model had him completing 61.4% of his passes, averaging 6.6 yards per attempt with an 82.1 passer rating.

Which brings us back to Goff and Jackson.

They started their careers headed in opposite directions, yet both eventually became two of the NFL's best quarterbacks. Goff didn't reach his current level until Detroit surrounded him with a strong offensive line, dependable running game and playmakers (and early on, Ben Johnson). Baltimore built its offense around Jackson's unique abilities rather than asking him to become something he wasn't.

The Raiders already have their quarterback of the future. Mendoza has eight games to show what he can do, but whether he goes 0-8, 6-2 or somewhere in between won't tell us much about the quarterback he could become. His job is to prove he belongs. The organization's job is to make sure he has a chance to succeed.

#2521. NFL trade deadline winners and losers: Kirk Cousins heads home, Bengals seemingly fail to understand the rules

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The 2026 NFL trade deadline has come and gone, and while we did see a couple of blockbuster trades in recent weeks, such as the Chicago Bears trading for Jeffery Simmons and the Jacksonville Jaguars swinging deals for three players in one day, the final 24 hours of the trade deadline were relatively quiet.

On Tuesday, the Minnesota Vikings brought back Kirk Cousins to replace Kyler Murray, and the Kansas City Chiefs added a new wide receiver in Josh Downs. However, there were plenty of other teams perceived to be "buyers" who stayed put, while other "sellers" were hesitant to part ways with their assets. In all, 23 teams combined to make 18 trades with 19 players and 34 picks changing hands. It was the Indianapolis Colts who led the way with an NFL-high four trades for six draft selections, although star running back Jonathan Taylor was not moved.

So, who won and who lost at the trade deadline? Let's take a look.

The Vikings and Las Vegas Raiders made the deal of the day, as new general manager Nolan Teasley sent a third-round pick to "Sin City" for Kirk Cousins. It feels like everyone is a winner in this situation.

The Vikings are a winner because they absolutely had to do something at the quarterback position. Kyler Murray wasn't cutting it, and then Carson Wentz registered one of the worst performances by a Vikings quarterback ever on Monday night with an 8.9 passer rating and a 32% completion rate. The Vikings were wasting the efforts of the best defense in the NFL and found themselves in a spot where they were forced to make an addition. Bringing back a familiar face who has been performing well this season with 20 touchdowns and eight interceptions is a good move.

Cousins actually has the most passing touchdowns (20) and career passing touchdowns (318) by a quarterback changing teams midseason, all-time. During his six seasons in Minnesota (2018-2023), he ranked top five in completion percentage, passing yards and passing touchdowns while going 50-37-1 as the starter.

The Raiders are a winner because they got a third-round pick for their rental quarterback in a season where they likely aren't making the playoffs. The Vikings didn't enter this year expecting to trade for a quarterback in November, which allowed the Raiders to drive up the price.

Kirk Cousins is a winner because he upgrades his own situation. He goes from 4-5 to 6-2, and has the opportunity to spark a legitimate Super Bowl run. That may sound like an exaggeration, but with Justin Jefferson, Jordan Addison and T.J. Hockenson, the Vikings have everything in place to make a run. All they needed was better quarterback play. It could be a storybook ending for Cousins.

Fernando Mendoza is a winner because he's the new starter in Vegas, although the No. 1 overall pick has to begin his NFL career against some aggressive defenses with the Seattle Seahawks on Sunday and then the Denver Broncos the following week.

Another winner is Justin Jefferson, because he gets his quarterback back. JJ began his NFL career with three straight 1,400-yard seasons — including a 1,809-yard campaign in 2022. Jefferson barely crossed 1,000 yards receiving last season. Now, he can suit up next to the best quarterback he's ever played with again. His 98.9 receiving yards per game when catching passes from Cousins are the most by a QB-WR duo all-time (min. 50 games).

Tuesday morning, it was reported that the Cincinnati Bengals were sending a sixth-round pick to the Philadelphia Eagles for pass rusher Arnold Ebiketie. This wouldn't have been a massive story, except the Bengals front office didn't realize they would also be giving up a third-round pick in the deal!

Nick Korte of Over The Cap pointed out that Ebiketie was signed as a compensatory free agent by the Eagles. The Bengals lost three compensatory free agents and signed two, with Cordell Volson not qualifying as a CFA lost since he hasn't played a snap this year. So, adding Ebiketie means the Bengals would lose a 2027 compensatory third-round pick that was coming after Trey Hendrickson signed with the Baltimore Ravens.

Oh that's brutal on the 3rd round comp pick! as noted by @nickkorte pic.twitter.com/OwwyNB71PA

From the NFL Collective Bargaining Agreement:

"If a Club trades for a player who was a CFA during that League Year, whether the player was another Club's CFA or the acquiring Club's own CFA, the player will be considered a CFA gained by the acquiring Club and will be included in the Compensatory netting process described above."

It's believed Cincinnati initially thought Volson counted toward the formula.

Naturally, when the Bengals discovered this, they backed out of the deal. This isn't even the first time Korte has had to correct the league about compensatory picks. He actually helped the Bengals secure a top-100 pick in the 2024 NFL Draft after a compensatory mix-up.

Duke Tobin and the Bengals look silly because they almost gave up a third-round pick for Ebiketie. They should hire Korte in the front office after helping them twice in three years.

There's no questioning the Jaguars' goal this season: They are all-in on a Super Bowl. Here's what they traded just this week:

Jacksonville saw Eric Murray go down with a season-ending injury, so they targeted Bates to replace him. He's tied for the second-most interceptions (28) since entering the league in 2018 and is the only NFL player to have recorded a pick-six in each of the last three seasons.

The Jaguars also lost defensive tackle DaVon Hamilton for the remainder of the season after he tore his quad, so the front office went out and acquired a couple of legitimate starters in Godchaux and Davis.

The Jaguars are "winners" because it's exciting when a team gets this aggressive and pushes all of their chips to the middle of the proverbial table. Fans have all the reason in the world to be excited about this run for the No. 1 seed in the AFC.

However, while Jacksonville's roster got better this week, I am questioning all the capital the Jags just spent.

Trading second- and fifth-round picks for Bates is expensive, but giving up first- and second-round picks for Davis was shocking. He's a solid player in the middle, but no one had any idea the Eagles would fetch that kind of return for him. He's recorded 31 tackles and 1.5 sacks in nine games played this season, and he recorded a career-high 4.5 sacks in 2025. Just eight months ago, Davis signed a three-year, $78 million extension that made him one of the highest-paid defensive tackles in the NFL.

If the Jaguars win the Super Bowl, then we can't complain about the compensation. But Jimmy James Gladstone is clearly in an "eff them picks" mood.

2027 second-round pick, 2028 fifth-round pick

2027 first-round pick, 2029 second-round pick

There was a lot of oxygen given to running backs at this year's trade deadline. The Colts' Jonathan Taylor was a player everyone was watching, the Ravens' Derrick Henry was another big name brought up in rumors, theTennessee Titans' Tony Pollard was viewed as a potential target and Breece Hall had seemingly fallen out of favor in New York with the emergence of Braelon Allen. However, not one running back was moved.

It's understandable if a team didn't want to trade a Christian McCaffrey-like package for Taylor, but what about Pollard? He shredded the Cleveland Browns for 129 yards and three touchdowns in Week 7, and then racked up 117 rushing yards and two touchdowns in Week 8 against the Bengals. He's averaging a career-high 74.4 rushing yards per game and ranks top 12 in rushing yards and rushing touchdowns this season. Pollard and Henry are the only players to have rushed for 1,000 yards in each of the last four seasons. Isn't that worth a fourth-round pick?

There were multiple Super Bowl or playoff hopefuls that could have used a new running back, such as the Vikings, Broncos, Green Bay Packers and New York Giants. Instead, Taylor, Henry, Pollard and Hall will continue running the ball for teams that won't be playing meaningful football in January.

The Chiefs have the No. 2 offense in the NFL through nine weeks, but this passing attack has struggled. They needed to make an addition at wide receiver at the trade deadline, and Brett Veach did just that by trading a fourth-round pick and a fifth-round pick to the Colts for Josh Downs and a seventh-rounder.

Downs has recorded the second-most receiving yards from the slot (1,995) since 2023, trailing only Amon-Ra St. Brown. While he's not exactly a "field stretcher" that is going to slice through defenses for 40-yard bombs, he still upgrades this passing offense.

Mahomes is actually the only quarterback in the past 20 years to average under 5.0 air yards per attempt in four straight games (min. 30 attempts).

The 5-2-1 Giants are the clear-cut frontrunners in one of the worst divisions in the NFL. However, John Harbaugh hasn't clinched the division just yet. The Giants did swing a trade for a new quarterback in J.J. McCarthy, but they were also interested in adding a star defensive tackle like Jeffery Simmons or a running back like Jonathan Taylor. Instead, they remained quiet on Tuesday.

We'll see if Cam Skattebo can carry this rushing attack for the remaining nine games and if the Giants can finish atop this weird NFC East. But Giants fans wanted to see Harbaugh make an addition on Tuesday.

The Eagles traded away two starters in the past few weeks, defensive tackle Jordan Davis and offensive lineman Cam Jurgens. Remember, they also traded star wideout A.J. Brown to the New England Patriots in June.

When you count up all the capital the Eagles acquired for those three players, Philly received two first-round picks, two second-round picks and two fifth-round picks. That's comparable to the Ricky Williams trade between Washington and New Orleans back in 1999.

Two 1st-round picks, two 3rd-round picks, 4th-round pick, 5th-round pick, 6th-round pick, 7th-round pick

Jordan Davis, Cam Jurgens, A.J. Brown haul

Two 1st-round picks, two 2nd-round picks, two 5th-round picks

One team that should have been in the running for Downs along with the Chiefs was the Los Angeles Rams. Davante Adams is on injured reserve with a hamstring injury, Puka Nacua is expected to join him with a knee issue, and Jordan Whittington was just placed on injured reserve due to a back injury. That means Tutu Atwell, Konata Mumpfield and CJ Daniels are Matthew Stafford's top receivers.

The 5-4 Rams are not the "Super Team" many thought they would be in 2026, and they didn't make any moves at the trade deadline in an attempt to right the ship. Sean McVay will try to grind out wins through Kyren Williams, Blake Corum and his tight ends.

The Jaguars orchestrated multiple trades to boost their roster with sights set on the No. 1 seed in the conference. How were the Buffalo Bills going to respond? On Tuesday, Brandon Beane sent a second-round pick to the Titans for safety Amani Hooker and a fifth-round pick.

Hooker has been a beast as of late. He powered the Titans to their first win of the season against the Colts with 13 tackles and an interception, then picked off Joe Burrow THREE times in Week 8. Hooker is just the third player in the past 40 years to begin a season with 40 tackles and five interceptions through seven games.

Following the release of C.J. Gardner-Johnson, the Bills needed to make an addition on the back end, and Hooker fits the bill. It was a pricey move, but I respect the swing from a Super Bowl-or-bust team.

Jaguars wide receiver Brian Thomas Jr. was viewed as a prime trade candidate this year, but he's staying put in Jacksonville. A change of scenery could have done him some good, but BTJ will just have to deal with being WR4 behind Parker Washington, Jakobi Meyers and Josh Cameron. His 117 yards receiving through nine weeks rank No. 7 on the team.

Remember, back in 2024, Thomas became the fourth rookie to record 1,200 yards receiving and catch double-digit touchdowns, joining Randy Moss, Odell Beckham Jr. and Ja'Marr Chase. However, he's quickly fallen out of favor in Jacksonville. Thomas has played just 43.1% of offensive snaps this season and has caught zero passes in three out of the last four games.

We saw two big-name defensive tackles traded this cycle in Jeffery Simmons and Jordan Davis. The Bears sent the Titans two first-round picks and a Day 3 pick swap for Simmons, while Davis went from Philly to Jacksonville for a first-round pick and a second-round pick.

Forget pass rushers, defensive tackles are the new premium position! There have been five first-round picks traded for veteran defensive tackles in the past two seasons. There have been just six first-round picks traded for all other veteran players in that same timeframe. Simmons, Davis, Dexter Lawrence and Quinnen Williams are the interior linemen who went for first-round picks in the last 365 days.

#2520. Felix Nmecha breaks silence on controversial crown celebration

Germany sporting director Rudi Völler announced on Monday that he intends to hold talks with Borussia Dortmund midfielder Felix Nmecha following the controversy surrounding his goal celebration over the weekend.

After getting on the scoresheet in Dortmund's 2-1 win over SV Elversberg, Nmecha kneeled down, removed an imaginary crown and placed it on the ground – a celebration he had also performed after scoring for Germany in their 7-1 win over Curaçao at last summer's World Cup.

The celebration has been associated with the evangelical network “Ballers in God”, which LGBTQ+ organisations have described as “Christian fundamentalist”, and its campaign “The King's Return”.

According to research by, among others, ARD's Monitor programme, parts of the religious group hold homophobic and anti-LGBTQ+ views and describe abortion as “Satan's plan”.

However, Nmecha has now taken to Instagram to clarify the meaning behind his celebration, insisting that he was not seeking to promote any organisation, discrimination or hate, but rather to express his faith in Jesus.

“It has been brought to my attention that my recent goal celebration has led to some misunderstandings,” Nmecha wrote.

"My celebration is not intended to promote myself or any organization. Rather, it is about laying my "crown" before the soon coming King and pointing to Jesus, my hope and strength!

"My message has never been about promoting intolerance, discrimination, or hate in any form.

"As Christians, our message is one of love and respect for everyone, regardless of where they come from, what they believe, or what their worldview may be.

“For God so loved the world..”, John 3:16," he concluded.

Nmecha is part of Germany's squad for the upcoming fixtures against Serbia on November 13 and the Netherlands on November 16.

#2519. Mjällby AIF: An Analysis of the Swedish Champions’ Possession Play – MH

von Next Generation am 23.12.2025 in den Kategorien Team Portraits mit 1 Kommentar

Mjällby AIF are Swedish champions. For the first time in their history, the small fishing village of 1,300 inhabitants has managed to outperform the competition from the bigger cities, helped by an exceptional brand of attacking football.

“Europe’s surprise team comes from a tiny fishing village on Sweden’s southern coast. The sporting director is a farmer. The coach is a former school principal. The story of Mjällby AIF: a miracle?“ – Dorfklub Mjällby AIF mischt Schweden auf: Einsame Spitze – 11FREUNDE

”A unique tale in football: In Sweden, Mjällby AIF from a small fishing village and with little money are celebrating the championship, thanks in part to the football doctor.“ – Mjällby AIF: Der Meister aus dem Fischerdorf | DIE ZEIT

“Not even ten years ago, the village club stood on the brink of collapse. This weekend, Mjällby could become the smallest place ever to produce a European champion.“ – Mjällby könnte Meister werden: Bekommt Schweden einen Sensationsmeister – 11FREUNDE

“Always follow the beach, then turn left at the campsite. Anyone heading for the stadium of league leaders Mjällby AIF in the Swedish fishing village of Hällevik won’t struggle to find it. ‘We play where the world ends and the sea begins’ is how the club describes the route to their home ground that bears the lovely name Strandvallen.“ – Fußball: Warum der Dorfklub Mjällby AIF Meister in Schweden werden könnte | sportschau.de

“For Mjällby’s opponents, a trip to the far south of Sweden feels like a journey to the Earth’s end. ‘When teams come on here on the bus they drive and drive, through the farms, past the fishing harbours,’ says Hasse Larsson. ‘They keep driving and then, when they can’t drive any further, they find our stadium.’” – Mjällby making minor miracles in an extraordinary Swedish football story | European club football | The Guardian

“’It’s 1,500 inhabitants in the village where they play, and you’re just flabbergasted when you see this elite football going on,’ Erik Hadzic – a reporter for TV4 Fotbollskanalen, who has covered the team for the last five years – tells CNN Sports. ‘Mjällby winning the Swedish championship is arguably the biggest sensation in the history of the Swedish league.’ The tiny team from Hällevik has not just won the league, either. It has absolutely blown away the competition.” – Mjällby AIF: How a tiny Swedish team achieved one of the biggest ever shocks in European soccer | CNN

Mjällby AIF have managed to appear across virtually every media outlet. By winning the Swedish championship, the small village club now enter Champions League qualifying, giving them the chance to measure themselves against the very biggest. This article aims to explain the type of football that led Mjällby to the Swedish title. Since their possession game stands out, the analysis focuses exclusively on this aspect.

Assistant coach Dr Karl Marius Aksum is regarded as the main architect of Mjällby’s attacking football. In his doctoral thesis, he wrote about visual perception and more specifically about scanning in professional footballers. Scanning is defined there as “all head movements away from the ball with the intention of gathering performance related information from one’s surroundings.” Aksum uses Gibson’s ecological theory of perception to show why scanning matters.

This theory emphasises that perception is inseparable from action possibilities. Humans do not only perceive objects, but above all the possibilities for action that an environment offers them, known as affordances. Translated into a football context: only when a player recognises the relevant elements of a situation, such as an opponent’s position, a passing option or a teammate’s run, can he make the appropriate decision. If such action possibilities remain unnoticed due to poor scanning, they will not be used.

Unlike most previous research on scanning in football, Aksum equipped players with specialised sports goggles using eye tracking technology, collecting data during full sided eleven versus eleven matches. These game realistic data allowed him to obtain results that reflect actual match conditions far more closely. The findings show that an average scan lasts roughly 0.40 seconds, although the most common scan duration is substantially shorter at 0.26 seconds. Moreover, 90.3 percent of all scans are shorter than 0.66 seconds. Fixations occur only rarely, as just 2.3 percent of scans contain a fixation and these last significantly longer than regular scans.

It is also highlighted that players do not process details such as faces in this short time frame, but mainly detect movements and colours. For training practice, this means that drills requiring prolonged or detailed information gathering during scanning lack match realism. In game situations, the brief duration of scans only allows players to pick up fundamental spatial and colour based cues. I have linked the dissertation here, titled ”Visual Perception in Elite Football“. The topic of scanning will also be examined in greater detail in another future article, possibly in a slightly different format.

Before Aksum’s arrival two years ago, Mjällby struggled heavily to turn matches around after falling behind. The club subsequently advertised a position aimed at solving this issue and succeeded. Karl Marius Aksum has since been appointed head coach for the 2026 season, taking over from the highly capable leader Anders Torstensson, who has moved into the role of technical director. Mjällby are now able to play through high pressing opponents as well as create chances against deep defensive blocks.

To conduct this analysis, I examined six different matches. Since six games are a limited sample and could skew certain aspects of the possession game, I list them here: Mjällby 4-1 Degerfors, AIK 2-1 Mjällby, Norrköpping 1-1 Mjällby, Mjällby 2-0 AIK, Malmö 1-3 Mjällby, Mjällby 2-0 Elfsborg.

The selection of matches was not made by me but by the aforementioned Karl Marius Aksum. I am therefore confident that these six fixtures cover the majority of Mjällby’s overall game. Many thanks once again for the openness. Obtaining suitable video material from the Allsvenskan turned out to be far more difficult than expected.

Mjällby generally operate in a nominal 1-3-2-4-1 structure. Goalkeeper Törnqvist is exceptionally strong with the ball at his feet. He is therefore consistently integrated into Mjällby’s build-up through a goalkeeper line. When Mjällby build with a back four, he can function as either the right or the left centre back. He very often looks for line breaking passes through the middle. His qualities have also caught the attention of Como, currently fifth in Serie A as of December 2025, who have already signed him. Como under coach Cesc Fàbregas also repeatedly build short with the goalkeeper involved.

The back three usually consists of right centre back Iqbal, central centre back Norén and left centre back Pettersson. Iqbal in particular pushed higher in certain matches during the build-up phase. Despite standing 1.92 metres tall, he is technically excellent and can therefore also take on the slightly higher and wider full back role of a back four depending on the opponent. Against deep defensive blocks, both outside centre backs of the back three are actively involved in the attacking phase. More on this later.

The wing backs in the five man line are Johansson on the right and Stroud on the left. Johansson is one of the more experienced players at 28 and among those with the most minutes. He frequently provides depth with runs beyond the opposition back line, combining pace with physical strength. He is also the first Mjällby player ever to be capped for the Swedish national team. Left wing back Stroud, on the other hand, was deployed centrally as a number ten towards the end of the season. Left wing back Stavitski is considered the primary replacement. The wing backs can operate at virtually any height and are used asymmetrically depending on the opponent. They often provide width when Mjällby attack with two wide players.

The centre of Mjällby’s structure is something of a holy grail in their build-up. In the nominal 1-3-2-4-1, it consists of two tens and two sixes, but only nominally. To gain a clearer understanding of Mjällby’s build-up, I eventually began to describe the structures as for example 1-3-diamond-w2-d1 (w=wide, d=deep), 4-trapezoid-1-w2, 1-3-Y-2-d1 and so on. By isolating the centre as a separate perspective, the different central configurations become particularly visible. Depending on build-up height and the opponent, Mjällby vary the number and positioning of their tens, eights and sixes. What stays constant is that there are always four central players. The w2 notation (w=wide) refers to the wing backs, though not perfectly accurate since they can also abandon the wide corridor.

Six Gustavsson is essentially always part of the central unit. He plays from the deepest central role, close to the defensive line, and is the team’s captain. Until his departure in the summer, the technically gifted six or eight Rojkjaer was also a constant. He was replaced depending on the opponent by various players, such as eight Thorell, left wing back Stroud or ten Kjaer. On the right side as a ten or eight, Gustafson (not to be confused with six Gustavsson) usually features.

The left or central ten Manneh deserves special mention, as he brings exceptional qualities. He is explosive, very fast and excellent when driving forward on the dribble. Alongside wing back Johansson, Manneh regularly provides depth or beats opponents to create superiority. He is already being linked with clubs from the top two divisions in England. His output is all the more remarkable considering that Mjällby as a team rank lowest in the league for dribbles. Dribbling simply is not a frequently used attacking tool for them, yet Manneh consistently stands out.

Up front, the lone striker is usually the experienced Bergström. He is used as a target and is frequently the focal point in the build-up, laying balls off for advancing central players. On aerial deliveries, he is the primary target.

Mjällby’s possession game is not the only factor behind the Swedish champions’ success. Naturally, their play also includes several other interesting elements, such as ball-near overloads during opposition throw-ins or a strong central focus in their pressing. In attack, they also make frequent use of long throw-ins into the box, and set pieces play an important role. The possession game, however, is one of the most intriguing in Europe, as it operates with completely different structures and patterns than usual. Accordingly, the focus of this team analysis lies on this aspect.

Mjällby’s build-up structure varies significantly depending on the opponent’s pressing approach. This naturally creates challenges for the analysis. While there are overarching principles, these do not lead to fixed or repetitive patterns. On the contrary, Mjällby’s build-up looks particularly different when facing a high press or full man marking on goal kicks. The main differences arise from the structures and target zones Mjällby uses to exploit specific weaknesses in the opponent’s pressing. For this reason, the following analysis of the build-up will be broken down by match.

Mjällby started, as usual, from a 3-2-4-1. There was, however, an important detail in the central area. With Bang-Kittilsen and Manneh, two natural number 10s were fielded, meaning that Gustafson – another 10/8 profile – occupied the nominal holding midfielder role. Depending on the phase of play, Mjällby could therefore rely on three number 10s and build from a one-three structure in midfield.

Degerfors pressed in a 5-4-1, shifting into a 5-2-3 during the high press. As is common in the Swedish league, they avoided full man marking and instead maintained a plus-one or plus-two advantage in the last line. Consequently, Degerfors did not press goalkeeper Törnqvist directly, but triggered their press after the first pass. Because both Degerfors midfielders pushed high to avoid being outnumbered centrally, a large space opened between their midfield and defensive line. In addition, the half backs in the Degerfors back three did not step forward into this space but held their position on the last line to provide cover.

Mjällby build up from a 4-trapezoid-3 structure and look to transition into three number tens in order to exploit the large space between the lines in Degerfors’ 5-4-1 pressing shape.

Mjällby’s obvious objective was therefore to exploit this large space between the lines. Using the goalkeeper as an extra player and with three number 10s available, they were well equipped to access and run through that zone. The starting point for the build-up against Degerfors was the 4-trapezoid-3. Fullbacks Stroud and Johansson pushed up to the level of striker Bergström, engaging the wingbacks of the opposition’s back five.

A typical feature of Mjällby’s build-up against a more passive high press or high block is their narrow four-man first line. The two outer centre backs spread roughly to the width of the penalty-area edges. The central centre back (usually on the left) and the goalkeeper (usually on the right) form the inner pair of this line. The extreme narrowness of this four-man row is notable. While many top European teams build with a slightly wider back three, Mjällby positions four players in a tight horizontal line.

The aim, beyond achieving numerical superiority, is likely to enable passing routes around the pressing block. Through the flat and narrow positions of the nominal fullbacks in the first line and the high positioning of Johansson and Stroud, the entire wing channel is opened. Typically, one of the central midfielders drops into that space to become available. The passing angle into the wide channel is optimal because the dropping player does not need to move all the way toward the touchline. Instead, he can remain closer to the centre, with shorter distances and better conditions to play back inside.

Due to the narrow back four in the build-up and the high positioning of the full-backs, the number tens can receive the ball around the block without having to drop all the way out to the touchline.

The heart of the build-up in this match lay in the central area. The basic structure was a trapezoid shape with the initially narrower positions of the sixes, Gustafson and Gustavsson, and the slightly wider starting points of the 10s, Bang-Kittilsen and Manneh. To continuously generate new passing options, Gustafson, Bang-Kittilsen and Manneh constantly searched for fresh open lanes and spaces to position themselves in. Initially, Gustafson often pushed deep into the large space between the lines, which prompted the two other 10s to adjust and occupy alternative passing lanes. This created constant rotation and caused problems for Degerfors.

From Degerfors’ perspective, they were outnumbered centrally against Mjällby’s four central players. When one of the 10s attacked a lane through the pressing block, another central player reacted by creating a passing option around the block. By dropping and offering an outlet outside the pressing trap, Degerfors faced a dilemma. If they closed the passing lane to the dropping midfielder, they opened a new channel through the centre. As a result, Mjällby repeatedly managed to open new passing routes and break the press through the rotating midfielders. The same logic applied in their build-up against Degerfors’ mid block, which will be examined again in that section, this time supported with an additional graphic.

Mjällby operated in this match primarily from a 3-diamond-w2-d1 structure. The diamond in midfield was formed by captain Gustavsson as the six, Rojkjaer (a six in the 3-4-2-1) as the left eight, Gustafson (a ten in the 3-4-2-1) as the right eight, and Manneh as the ten. In contrast to the match against Degerfors, the fullbacks Stroud and Johansson were not supposed to remain permanently on the height of the last line. Instead, they dropped towards the ball on the outside lane especially when AIK managed to put pressure on the outer centre back in the build-up. As a general rule, Mjällby’s fullbacks act as the width providers in the build-up against a high-pressing opponent.

AIK used pure man marking in both the high press and on goal kicks. Unlike Mjällby’s other opponents, AIK did not maintain a plus-one in the last line. Instead, one of their centre backs directly engaged ten Manneh. In addition, AIK’s defenders repeatedly pushed forward aggressively from behind onto the Mjällby midfielders in a man-marking manner to prevent any free player from emerging. This had the major advantage of not having to press in numerical inferiority in the centre.

However, Mjällby managed particularly in the first 15 minutes to escape the man marking through a flat build-up. To achieve this, Mjällby used very flat eights and a ball-near fullback dropping towards the play. This created a kind of 5(GK)-3-1-2 structure, with one high fullback acting as the far-side striker and the other fullback staying flat as the ball-near option. The space between the lines was opened, with only ten Manneh positioned there, allowing him to exploit his strengths in larger spaces.

Mjällby’s 4-3-1-1-w2 with asymmetrical full-backs against AIK’s man-oriented marking: by creating an overload behind his direct opponent, Rojkjaer forces one of AIK’s centre-backs to loosen the man-marking on Manneh in order to provide cover, which makes Manneh available to receive the ball.

Mjällby succeeded in the early phases whenever they managed to “loosen” the man marking of the AIK centre back on Manneh. For example, eight Rojkjaer ran into the expanded space between the lines behind his direct opponent. Because this created a brief numerical inferiority for AIK, their marking centre back instinctively dropped off, allowing Manneh to be found as the free player between the lines. In general, Mjällby aimed in the build-up to open the centre in order to find the passing lane from a building defender into Manneh between the lines or into Bergström on the last line.

The fundamental objective of Mjällby’s build-up is to find the free player and then switch to the far side. If possible, this is done diagonally through the centre. Against man marking, however, Mjällby naturally encounters problems. Especially after Mjällby’s 1–0 goal in the 10th minute, AIK increased their risk-taking and applied tighter and earlier man marking. Because Mjällby’s build-up relies on freeing the central free player through coordinated movements, they struggle against pure man marking, in which no such free player appears. This theme runs throughout the entire analysis of their build-up against high pressing and becomes particularly relevant after taking the lead, since opponents then tend to abandon their cover and their plus-one advantage in the last line.

Of course, Mjällby also has mechanisms against pure man marking. Against AIK, a clear 5-3-1-2 structure appeared in goal-kick situations. Right back Johansson dropped very deep, while left back Stroud moved into the centre and high into the second-striker line. The idea behind this recurring goal-kick structure was to force the opponent either into a 3-versus-3 without cover or to abandon their man marking and instead pull an additional covering player backwards.

Mjällby’s 5-3-1-2 with asymmetrical wing-backs against AIK’s man-oriented marking at goal kicks: counter-movements in the front line and a counter-pressing net created by supporting runners stepping up.

Because AIK chose pure man marking without a covering player when full man marking the goal kick, Mjällby often went long to one of the three advanced players, frequently fullback Stroud, who dropped into the opened wide channel and laid the ball off to the players running through. The runners (the three midfielders and the ball-near fullback from the 5-3 structure) tried both to create lay-off options and to form a counterpressing net to win second balls. It is generally noticeable that Mjällby, due to their strong central occupation in the build-up against high pressing, wins a large number of second balls after turnovers. This is also a key part of Mjällby’s build-up play.

At the same time, Mjällby prepared the long balls on goal kicks through opposite movements of the three forward players. Before the ball was played, they made horizontal opposite runs to loosen the man marking and to gain more space and time on the lay-off.

It is also noticeable that the tighter the opponent moves into man marking, the more frequently striker Bergström is used as a target player. Whenever Mjällby came under pressure, the ball was often played into Bergström, who with his back to goal could hold the ball and lay it off to the midfielders running beyond him. Mjällby repeatedly managed through the movements of their midfielders to open the central passing lane or the direct ball into striker Bergström. Against AIK, Bergström was often found diagonally by Johansson, the flat fullback, from the touchline, or directly through a flat throw from goalkeeper Törnqvist. Bergström also served as an additional target player on goal kicks alongside fullback or striker Stroud.

As the nominal holding midfielder Rojkjaer transferred to Danish top-flight club Nordsjaelland during the summer transfer window, he was replaced by number eight Thorell in the return match against AIK. Due to weather conditions, the Allsvenskan pauses during winter and is played throughout the summer, meaning departures can occur mid-season. On the left side of the back three, Pettersson started instead of Iqbal, maintaining the same role and positional profile. In attack, Johansson started in place of the usual first-choice striker Bergström.

In contrast to the first leg against AIK, Mjällby used a slightly different central structure. As left-sided eight Thorell positioned himself higher than six Gustavsson, and right-sided ten Gustafson operated even higher than Thorell, this shape can be described neither as a diamond nor as a trapezoid. The most accurate description is a “Y-structure”. This highly interesting structure consists of Thorell and Gustavsson staggered vertically and slightly horizontally, supported by two tens.

Due to the staggered positioning of the two number sixes, a kind of diagonal “Y” shape emerges in central areas. From this structure, a variety of counter-movements with changes of vertical levels can be created, which are particularly difficult to defend against in a man-oriented marking scheme.

The Y-structure offers several advantages, particularly against man marking. Crucially, the Y is not fully symmetrical in its initial positioning. Because Thorell as an eight always started slightly offset from six Gustavsson, he formed a diagonal either with the left or the right ten. From this diagonal, it becomes significantly easier to generate varied horizontal opposite movements combined with changes of level. These movements are especially difficult to defend in a man-marking system, as they disrupt the opponent’s structure and greatly extend pressing distances. Defensive handovers also become much more difficult, since the diagonal Y allows for a wide range of possible opposite movements with level changes.

The diagonal Y also provides additional advantages against non-man-marking pressing. From this structure, the build-up players can quickly occupy a variety of passing lanes, and central access can be opened through easily created lateral overloads. The shape is also beneficial for lay-off play. Because multiple vertical levels are occupied simultaneously, simple movements can create several different lay-off options. The vertical staggering also improves counterpressing, as immediate mutual cover is available in transition moments.

As a result, a wide variety of movements could be observed from Mjällby within this Y-structure, making the central organisation appear almost random at times. In particular, eight Thorell could be found in nearly every area of the pitch. It was also helpful that the central players frequently rotated positions and roles among themselves. Since each player interpreted the respective role slightly differently, the build-up became even harder for AIK to read. This allowed Mjällby to progress the ball successfully on numerous occasions. As the first half progressed, AIK were also less frequently able to maintain numerical equality on the last line, which in turn created an extra player in midfield for Mjällby.

In contrast to the first leg, AIK initially defended goal kicks with a plus-one advantage on the last line. On goal kicks, Mjällby attempted to build in a similar way to the first leg, using a 5-3-1-2 or 5-3-3 structure, with left back Stroud positioned more centrally and higher in the forward line, and right back Johansson remaining flat and wide in the five-man build-up line. In this match, however, ten Manneh was much more involved in the opposite movements used to prepare long balls, which explains the shift towards a 5-3-3 instead of a 5-3-1-2. The three forwards moved unpredictably before the long ball, aiming to loosen man marking, remain difficult to access directly, and gain more time and space for lay-offs to the players arriving from deeper positions.

After approximately eight minutes, AIK adjusted their four-versus-three advantage on the last line. From that point on, one of their defenders was ready to step out onto one of Mjällby’s eights. Notably, Mjällby did not immediately choose the long ball from the goalkeeper in response. Instead, they first triggered the press through a short build-up and then played through it. There were several different variants of how the central players could behave in these situations. For example, one side could be overloaded by all three central midfielders, opening a diagonal passing lane to the far side towards striker or ten Manneh.

Around the 55th minute, a successfully executed goal kick from the asymmetrical 5-3-3 structure led to a free kick, which subsequently resulted in Mjällby’s 1–0 goal. First, the press was triggered by two passes between the goalkeeper and a centre back. From the opposite movements of the forwards, two attackers dropped towards the ball while one ran in behind. One of the forwards, in this case Manneh, was found directly with a flat diagonal pass into this lane, allowing him to turn and access the far side around fullback Johansson. As I cannot provide the video material on this page for legal reasons, I have linked the sequence as a video on X:
