#2463. Gotham to host semifinal at 5k Icahn Stadium

The club was fined $10k for the condition of the field following their regular season finale

Following a week of uncertainty, Gotham will host Sunday’s semifinal against the Kansas City Current at Icahn Stadium on Randalls Island in Manhattan. Questions lingered over the availability of several potential semifinal venues, but in the end, Gotham moved the match due to field conditions at the club’s regular home, Sports Illustrated Stadium.

“Unfortunately, given the field conditions, we have made the extremely difficult decision to relocate our semifinal game to Icahn Stadium,” club governor Carolyn Tisch Blodgett said in a statement announcing the venue. “We exhausted every possible avenue before making this decision, and we are deeply disappointed that so many of our fans will now be unable to experience this moment alongside our team.”

Icahn Stadium holds approximately 5,000 fans. Gotham’s 13 games at Sports Illustrated this season averaged just over 9,000. One of two games not played at Sports Illustrated was at Icahn in July against the Reign. A crowd of 4,738 was announced, although many either left or never arrived due to storms that delayed the start.

Gotham played the last two weeks at Sports Illustrated and the surface became a talking point. Following Sunday’s quarterfinal, Reign coach Laura Harvey said it was the worst pitch she has ever been a part of, and said Gotham coach Juan Carlos Amoros apologized to her pregame for the condition of the field. Harvey also let it be known that Gotham were fined $10k for it following the regular season finale against the Royals.

A Gotham spokesperson declined to elaborate on Harvey’s claims but The Equalizer has independently confirmed the fine. And Amoros was contrite in his postgame comments.

“I feel the obligation to to almost apologize for the state of the pitch,” Amoros said. “I think at this level in this kind of game, as a league, and we should be having a better a better surface.”

Added Tisch Blodgett: “Our players deserve a playing surface that meets the standards of a professional semifinal, and our fans deserve the opportunity to support them. We have worked tirelessly to deliver on both and are disappointed that we cannot. We are grateful to Icahn Stadium for working with us on such short notice to ensure our team has a place to compete for a Championship spot on Sunday.”

Gotham has one more season at Sports Illustrated. They are scheduled to move to Etihad Stadium, currently under construction in Queens, for the 2028 season.

#2462. The tragic legend of Erasmo Iacovone, the man who made Taranto dream

With the exception of Prato, whose digits have been greatly inflated by Far East Asian immigration in recent decades, there’s just one name amongst the 23 most populous cities in Italy never to have been linked to a Serie A team: Taranto.

Taranto is a city of contrasts. Lying on the inner coast of the southern region of Apulia, it was founded as a Greek colony in the 8th century, and has since thrived on its fame of a city rich in ancient art and archeological remains, not to mention the beauty of its crystal-clear sea, its mild climate all year long, the freshness of its fish and the abundance of products sprouting from the sun-drenched earth surrounding the urban centre.

After World War Two, though, a nation torn apart by the fighting needed a boost to achieve the so-called “Italian economic miracle” of the 1960s, and everyone had to do their share. For Taranto, such a share took the shape of the Italsider steel mill unveiled by the head of state, Giuseppe Saragat, in 1965.

The biggest of its kind in Europe, with a pipeline to refurbish the country with Siberian gas, it blazed a trail to a new era for the city. It was an era comprised of state-of-the-art foundries, oil refineries, chemical works, cement plants and food-processing factories that, despite skyrocketing the city’s GDP, made the air a little heavier, the seawater a little blurrier, the sun a little hazier and, eventually, resulted, half a century down the line, in Taranto producing 92 percent of Italy’s dioxin.

No other event in the city’s long history has had such a social impact. Below a sky now half blue and half grey, a new, disenchanted and despairing kind of humanity felt, more than ever, the need for something capable of reuniting the city’s two souls. Something to hold on to in case Taranto’s essence were to slip away through the rusty grate at the end of a drain pouring effluent into the sea.

Taranto has always been a city fond of its football team, even without any major achievements to revel in. It’s always been all about identity paired with the pride in rallying together to represent the city at what was once known as the Stadio Salinella – from the name of the neighbourhood it embellishes with its presence. But there was something different in the 1977/78 season.

After a solid eight consecutive Serie B campaigns, the Ionians started off their ninth one in great fashion. If by January record-breaking Ascoli already had a foot in the top division, Taranto were one of the main candidates to follow suit, trailing the Bianconeri by a handful of points halfway through the season.

With the exception of a few additions in goalkeeper Željko Petrović, centre-back Stefano Dradi and inside-forward Franco Panizza, the roster was the same that had comfortably dodged relegation the season before, earning a solid ninth place on the table. The biggest difference was represented by Erasmo Iacovone, now at the height of his footballing maturity.

Within the class of ’52, the moustachioed striker had joined the year before from Mantova, bagging eight goals in 27 appearances during his first year in Apulia. By the halfway point of the 1977/78 campaign, he was already at nine. By no means was he the one with good feet up front, especially when compared to Franco Selvaggi, who would go on to win the World Cup in 1982, or Graziano Gori. He wasn’t particularly tall either, standing at a mere 1,74m, even though his outstanding elevation had allowed him to head home each one of the eight strikes he’d had to his name in the first year with the red and blues.

At first, thrifty chairman Giovanni Fico wasn’t convinced to spend all that money on him. It took assistant coach Tommaso De Pietri, who’d worked with Iacovone at Carpi in 1973/74, to persuade him that it was a bargain. Fico himself didn’t stay sceptical for too long either, as Iacovone flew higher than any of Novara’s centre-backs to score his first goal on the day of his debut in late October 1976.

And yet, the love Iacovone received from the city was never a matter of pure goalscoring ability. He was admired by those who recognised themselves in his gentle smile, his good manners and his genuine affection for Taranto.

Born in the diminutive town of Capracotta, perched atop the Molisian Appenines and covered with snow for the biggest part of the year, Erasmo was a simple man rather than a superstar. Way before that reassuring, brown moustache started to adorn his good-natured face, Iacovone’s father decided to move to Tivoli in order to ensure a better future for his family.

It was here that his son started to kick a ball around, something quite difficult to do on Capracotta’s climbs and descents. Before turning 20, he’d already joined the ranks of OMI Roma, the team of the capital’s steelworkers. It proved somewhat of an omen, given that it would need a working-class city like Taranto to bloom once and for all, after years spent wandering between Trieste, Carpi and Mantova with mixed success.

Few people are more suited to describe what did Iacovone mean for his adoptive city than Pasquale Martemucci and Luigi Di Bella, the minds behind passionerossoblu.it, the most comprehensive database on all things Taranto, from its foundation to today.

“Talking of Iacovone is no easy task. For we Tarantinos he’s been, and still is, a myth and a legend,” the two pointed out. “Just like all myths and legends, it’s hard to find the right words to describe him. You always run the risk of getting stuck in the banality of small-town parochialism, which can tarnish a memory that should be passed on to new generations that haven’t lived in the 1970s, when football meant everything for Taranto.

“Not just the team, but the whole city was known elsewhere thanks to his name. ‘Iaco Gol’, as we usually refer to him, embodies the history of an entire city that saw in him an occasion for rebirth and for the redemption of its territory. He also symbolises the role Taranto longed to play not only in Serie A, but also in civil society. The city had never had someone to make it immediately identifiable elsewhere. Iacovone was Taranto, and Taranto was Iacovone.”

The most iconic Iaco Gol moment of all came on 20 November 1977, when Taranto hosted regional rivals Bari in a packed Salinella. It wasn’t a boring match. Opportunities rained down copiously, but each of them either hit the woodwork or was denied by the goalkeepers.

On 73 minutes, just as the game looked bound for a scoreless draw, a two-touch free-kick for Taranto in the attacking third was taken so quickly that, when the ball ended up at Iacovone’s boots, the gap between him and the defensive line was so big that everyone would have encircled the referee asking him to resort to the VAR had the game been played at another point in history.

Despite this, Graziano De Luca’s black gloves were only centimetres away from Iacovone, ready to protect the goalmouth from all dangers. The Taranto poster boy stopped the ball nonchalantly then, just as the Bari custodian was rushing towards him, he impudently chipped it over his body, keeping the other foot firmly planted on the ground. Maybe he wasn’t as technically modest as everybody thought.

“His goals were scored by everybody. Whenever he kicked or headed the ball, the whole city was there to push it across the goal-line,” Martemucci and Di Bella recalled. “The goal he scored versus Bari was particularly unforgettable. They were our historic rivals, a team all of us hated. It seemed like that ball, dexterously lifted up in the sky, was never meant to end up in the goal. It left all the almost 30,000 people sitting in the stands with baited breath.

“They all stood up, trying to give strength to the leather sphere. They all envisioned the goal and then there was silence, something rarely seen in a football stadium. Then, just like a miracle, the ball started its descending parable, with the goalkeeper diving desperately.

“Finally, there was a liberating roar, a frenzy took hold of the bystanders, who were exchanging hugs and kisses with strangers that suddenly felt like family, for the sheer fact of being there. Iacovone scored, but it was the whole city who took the lead. It’s a memory made up of images and feelings that each of those present on that November Sunday has passed on to their children, just like a testament.”

When Cremonese visited Taranto on 5 February 1978, the Apulians came off a run of seven games without a win, yet thanks to their chemistry and to the presence of one of the league’s most promising forwards in Iacovone, they still were widely regarded as one of the main candidates for promotion – provided that they could change the tide immediately.

That’s why it was particularly harsh on Iacovone to see the clash with Cremonese end 0-0. Everything seemed to be against him that day. The woodwork denied him the joy of scoring on multiple occasions, and when he successfully aimed at the empty space between the goalposts, he found an inspired Alberto Ginulfi on his way, a former Serie A goalkeeper mostly remembered for the penalty he denied none other than Pelé in a 1972 friendly between Roma and Santos, then lightheartedly savouring the last season of his career.

That day, Iaco Gol’s pregnant wife Paola was off to Carpi, where the two had first met, for a gynaecological check-up. The air was heavy in the dressing room after the draw with Cremonese. His teammates tried to persuade Iacovone to join them for a stand-up comedy night in a restaurant immersed in the countryside near the small town of San Giorgio Ionico.

“You’ll feel better, you need to take your mind off the game,” they told him, understanding how frustrating it’d been for him to fire blanks for 90 minutes at a time when the team, and the city they represented, needed him the most.

But the 25-year-old wasn’t the kind of guy who looks forward to a night out, the tranquillity of his home way more tempting than a loud table filled with good wine and local delicacies. And home he went, because it was time to call Paola and ask her about the check-up.

“Don’t stay on the couch brooding over today’s game all night. Go out and have some fun,” she must have said to him before hanging up. A few hours later, Iacovone stepped out of his humble Citroën Dyane 6, license plate MO 215872, in the parking lot of La Masseria, more as a way to avoid letting down the people who cared for him than for the actual desire to be there. Around midnight, when his tipsy dining companions asked him to stay a little longer, he firmly refused and headed back to his car.

It was pitch dark. In such a road bereft of lampposts, nothing could help Iacovone – about to take the provincial road that would have led him back to Taranto – to notice small-time criminal Marcello Friuli aboard a stolen Alfa Romeo 2000 GT rushing towards him. The latter had just burst his way through a police checkpoint and was now driving at full speed with the headlights off. The impact was tremendous.

When the police found the body of the only victim, lying in a roadside ditch tens of metres from the car, they immediately recognised him. Iacovone, aged just 25, had passed away without any suffering as a result of a severe head trauma, the golden Virgin Mary medal still in his mouth, as it was typical of him whenever he got lost in thought.

A few hours later, the city woke up and realised that the man who’d allowed it to dream was gone forever. The Santissima Annunziata Hospital, where the body was first stored, became a pilgrimage of sorts. The following day, Taranto came together to mourn its adopted son at the Robert Bellarmine Church.

Then, Iacovone was granted one last appearance at the Salinella, which would take on his name two days later by the will of chairman Fico. The latter was amongst the most touched after by tragedy, his soul quivering with remorse for having turned down Fiorentina’s bid for his best player a few weeks earlier. “Players are just like sons,” he stated, his voice broken with sorrow. “But you were even more, and now you’re with our Lord. As long as I’ll be alive, this stadium will be called by your name.”

The team never fully recovered from such a blow. Taranto was deprived not only of their top-scorer, but also of their guiding light, the man whose lifestyle, grit and kind heart everybody felt represented by; the player whose shirt every kid wanted to wear; the forward who made the sun above Taranto shine a little brighter every time he flew next to it to head the ball into the net.

From then on, the grey sky standing above Taranto’s industrial area took over the rest of this now dispirited city. It filtered through the soul of its inhabitants and undermined the spirit of its footballers. Form dipped and the Ionians ended up eighth, falling agonisingly short of their Serie A dreams.

In subsequent decades, the club mostly wandered through Serie B and a couple of league levels below it, never again coming close to such heights as they did in the Iaco Gol era. A statue unveiled in October 2002 at the entrance of the Stadio Erasmo Iacovone – financed through 13,000 donations of €1.50 each – is something a true hero deserves, and pays homage to the joy and the desperation Taranto has gone through for the love of its dear Erasmo.

“Those who were out of town for work or study reasons would have jumped through hoops to be at the Salinella on Sunday afternoon,” the founders of passionerossoblu.it reminisced. “On Wednesday night, there were people already lining up in front of the ticket offices to get their hands on a ticket, so that they could see the game and cheer with him. Then the day of such a tragic fatality came. With his demise, the whole city slipped back into a never-ending greyness, aware that it would have taken years to lift up once again. Iacovone has been all this.”

#2461. Aspect analysis: Leipzig never found a trigger – LC

von Next Generation am 20.10.2026 in den Kategorien Uncategorized mit 0 Kommentaren

A 6-1 reads like a game in which everything fell apart. Look at how the goals came about one by one and a different picture emerges: it was not six separate problems but two or three, which Bayern punished in seven variations. No pressure on the man in possession, marking problems in central areas, and a back line that did not work with the movements in front of it – that chain runs through practically every goal conceded.

This aspect analysis therefore takes the goals rather than the game as its material and works back from there to the patterns.

Bayern triggered very high throughout, stayed tight to their opponents and pushed through centrally without hesitation. Vandevoordt was pressed from Bayern’s right, with the clear intention of keeping him away from the left-hand build-up route and forcing the long ball. Leipzig’s front line of Nusa and Brajan Gruda repeatedly angled their runs deep against Nathaniel Brown and Konrad Laimer.

Bayern had one extra central player dropping into midfield in this phase, usually Kimmich. Had Leipzig played short to the right, he could have pressed through onto Raum; in practice he stayed central and pushed through from there. That left Leipzig with the long ball, and it was ineffective: it produced almost no regains, so the enforced forward play brought neither relief nor territory.

Going the other way, Leipzig got no access at all, and the reason was Bayern’s rotations. Kimmich dropped right, Pavlović left into a back three, with Upamecano holding a very wide position. Against this shifting three-man build-up Leipzig never found a trigger, because the assignments reset with every rotation – whoever was supposed to step out of midfield first had to work out who he was picking up. The handover of pressing duties out of central areas failed repeatedly.

In front of that, Bayern staggered their shape so that Leipzig’s compactness became the problem. Olise moved into the ten space at times, Nathaniel Brown operated in the half-lane and ran beyond from there, Luis Díaz stayed wide left. Saibari and Kane pinned several opponents centrally while regularly pulling out of the central lane. Because Leipzig pressed very narrow, this produced exactly what Bayern were looking for: once the opponent was committed near the ball, the switch followed, and on the now open side stood a one-on-one.

That already builds the bridge to the goals. The isolated one-on-ones in which Luis Díaz got his three finishes were not individual moments but the product of this sequence of pinning and switching.

1-0, Luis Díaz (12.) – The first goal already contains the full diagnosis. Kimmich receives centrally without any pressure and can turn out with an open body shape. Ahead of him Saibari and Kane occupy the central zone in front of the box, which forces Orban and Lukeba to step out – so far, the intended part. The full-backs, however, do not push up with that movement and stay too deep, while Raum’s position plays the runner onside. Klostermann stays outside and leaves the inside lane unsecured, and that is exactly where Luis Díaz starts from. Out of that unprotected lane Díaz runs into the back line and Kimmich chips the ball in behind. Not one bad decision, but four players whose decisions did not fit together.

2-0, Aleksandar Pavlović (26.) – Same cause, different route. Kane drops deep and Leipzig do not shift across as a unit – the reactions showed it clearly: arms thrown up, gesturing, hands dropping again, the beginnings of frustration. Kane gets the free body shape, and with him the consequence is predictable: the long ball, high or flat. Because Leipzig are so narrow centrally, the ball flies straight through the entire zone in front of their back line. Luis Díaz moves actively into the passing lane to control it while Klostermann tries to get into his running line and does not make it – Díaz reaches the ball first. From the one-on-one he wins, Díaz dribbles centrally at Orban, which creates a four-against-three on the break. Díaz pins Orban and Lukeba centrally, Pavlović overlaps on the left after holding a high, left-leaning position all evening and threatening the back line. Two touches, left foot, finished away from the defender.

3-0, Michael Olise (34.) – Here Bayern’s press shows itself at its clearest. From a Leipzig throw-in, the man-orientation is fully visible: consistent pushing through, clean handovers. A misplaced pass from Raum then cannot be defended, because neither the tracking nor the duelling is good enough to disturb the pass. Kane can open up half-way. Centrally, Olise comes inside from the wing, and Banzuzi and his partner fail to pick him up, letting him run through – against a player of that variability, an invitation to the key pass. Luis Díaz runs beyond and drags Orban with him, Klostermann is pinned wide by Saibari and can no longer get back into central areas. Olise finishes against the goalkeeper’s movement, across his standing leg into the far corner, catching Vandevoordt completely on the wrong foot.

4-0, Luis Díaz (47.) – After a regain, Bayern switch quickly to the far side and once diagonally through, putting Díaz in a one-on-one again. He holds the ball in the dribble, and Leipzig fail to solve the situation in three steps: the centre is not closed, Orban is too late stepping out, Klostermann does not get into the duel. That Vandevoordt leaves the far corner open is the final piece of an isolated one-on-one that should never have arisen.

5-0, Harry Kane (53.) – Structurally the most interesting goal. Leipzig play a long ball without preparing it and react to the consequences contradictorily: the back line does not push up at all, while the midfield line and both forwards counterpress forwards. The ten space opens up enormously, the gaps between the lines become huge – and Olise is standing in that zone. One pass from Kim is enough to take six Leipzig players out of the game. Olise runs unopposed at the back line and lays it off to Díaz, who is in a one-on-one again; Brown joins for the two-against-one and shifts into the inside lane. Klostermann does not pick up his run from the deep half-space, and centrally Kane again drops into Orban’s blind side – a pattern that stood out across the whole game. The result is a two-against-one against the goalkeeper.

6-0, Luis Díaz (69.) – From a set piece Bayern create a five-against-four out wide. Gnabry pins opponents and makes the space for Díaz, Orban again takes one big step in the block and does not get into the duel. The same scene as the 4-0, only from a different phase of play – a sign that this is a behavioural pattern rather than a snapshot.

6-1, Andrija Maksimović (90.+1) – Leipzig’s goal shows in reverse what their own game had been missing. Bayern drop into a deeper block here, and Leipzig combine centrally before going wide. Gruda gets into a one-on-one against Brown, Upamecano steps across – but from above, with too wide a gap and without closing the centre. That opens the one-two, which Leipzig take immediately. Because the whole situation narrows onto that combination, the space behind it stays unoccupied, and Maksimović can take two touches on his left and finish unopposed.

The sequence of goals reads like a repetition. Five of Bayern’s six come from the same combination of no pressure on the ball centrally and a back line that does not manage the space behind it. Luis Díaz stands in an isolated one-on-one three times, Orban is twice too late with a step that is too big, Kane repeatedly drops into his blind side. Klostermann certainly did not have his best day – but it would be too easy to settle the bill with him. In the decisive scenes he faced situations that functioning protection in front of him should never have allowed to arise in the first place.

Behind it all lies not an individual problem but a structural one: Leipzig pressed narrow and found no trigger against Bayern’s rotating back three. That very compactness made the switch of play the opponent’s most effective tool, and at the end of every switch stood a one-on-one that Leipzig lost. The scoreline is not the story – the story is that the same scene worked six times.

LC is often found in a classroom, happiest on a football pitch, and occasionally on LinkedIn.

#2457. Pelé at the 1970 World Cup: the memories beyond the goals

Every four years, strikers from a host of countries converge on that ultimate festival of football: the World Cup. For many, this represents the pinnacle of their careers to date, the chance to prove themselves against the best and to write themselves into history. And each World Cup throws up a forward who is forever associated with that competition; often one goal in particular that lives on in collective memories.

Go right back to 1962 and we see Garrincha score a thundering shot against England in the quarter-finals. 1966 sees an exhausted Geoff Hurst hurtle towards goal before unleashing a piledriver past Hans Tilkowski – a shot that he later admitted was hit as hard as it was so that if he likely missed, it would eat up time recovering the ball.

In 1974, Gerd Muller shows his predatory instincts to spin on a dime and cause Dutch heartache. Four years later, Mario Kempes bursts through the Netherlands defence, hair billowing behind him. The list goes on: Paolo Rossi in 1982 against Brazil; Diego Maradona in 1986 against England; Roberto Baggio in 1990 against Czechoslovakia.

What these all have in common is forwards scoring goals that are forever remembered from those respective tournaments and often the first thing that you will think off when someone mentions their name and the competition. If I simply say the words 1998 and Zinedine Zidane, it’s likely your first thought is of his two goals in the final.

The list above has deliberately excluded one World Cup, the 1970 edition in Mexico. Yes that beautiful World Cup that was the first in colour with the shimmering heat haze and crackling commentary. And if you play the word association game once again and ask someone what first pops into their head when you mention that competition, the likely answer is Brazil.

Indeed, if you then ask them to name one player from that team, it is odds on they are going to say Pelé. Because while the Brazil side that won the tournament were arguably the greatest national team of all time (Hungary 1954 and the Netherlands 1974 might like to debate that), one player still managed to stand out from such illustrious company.

Just how great a striker was Pelé? Well, let’s start with 501 goals in 493 appearances for Santos between 1956 and 1974 – so yes, averaging a goal a game for 18 years. Ah, but I hear you say, ‘that is in the Brazilian league, which surely is not the same standard as European leagues?’ That is open to debate, particularly given the number of world-class footballers within the competition at the time.

Let’s then consider Pelé’s international record of 77 goals in 92 games. That includes playing in four World Cups against the top teams of those times. Faced with statistics such as those, it is hard not to argue that Pelé was extremely good at putting the ball into the net.

But that leads to an interesting observation. There is no doubt that the 1970 World Cup and Pelé are intertwined in people’s memories. One of the greatest goalscorers of all-time helped his side lift the trophy with four goals across the tournament, but oddly enough if you again ask people the first five things that come into their head when you say Pelé and 1970, I think you would be surprised to find that not a single one of them would be a goal scored by him.

Unlike the other strikers mentioned earlier, Pelé’s fame in 1970 actually came more from misses than goals. Yes, one of the greatest goalscorers is actually remembered better for misses and saves.

Brazil’s opening match of the tournament sees them pitted against a decent Czechoslovakia team. The game is only three minutes old when a ball across the area finds Pelé unmarked in front of an open goal, who then proceeds to place the ball over the bar. That miss is then compounded by the Czechs having the cheek to take the lead after just 11 minutes. Things are not going according to plan. But Brazil begin to regain their composure and, after 23 minutes, Rivellino thunders in a trademark free-kick.

As half-time approaches, Pelé receives the ball within the Brazil half and surveys the scene while moving slowly towards the centre circle. Then, suddenly, he smashes the ball goalwards. As the camera follows the flight of the ball, it picks up the Czech goalkeeper, Ivo Viktor, furiously backpedalling. In that split second after receiving the ball, Pelé has noticed Viktor has strayed forward from his goalline and decided to attempt to lob him. The Brazilian commentator describes the action perfectly: “Pele, Pele, Pele … almost,” as the ball just goes wide of the post.

It is important to bear in mind the context of this attempt. This is not a league match against Wimbledon where you are 2-0 up in injury time, so why the hell not have a go; this is an opening World Cup tie in which you are level. To even attempt such a lob on such a stage shows the audacity of Pelé. That is strengthened by the fact that, even though he actually missed, it is still remembered by all. Yes, David Beckham’s lob was fantastic, but he was standing on the shoulders of Pele.

Brazil end up with an emphatic 4-1 victory over Czechoslovakia, including a goal from Pelé before being overshadowed by a double from Jairzinho. But they face stiff competition in their group by being drawn alongside the reigning champions England, who arguably have a better team now than in ’66. And so the second match of the group between the two teams is always going to be critical in terms of who advances top.

The game kicks off at noon under a scorching Mexican sun – advantage Brazil in terms of weather. Just seeing a red-headed, freckled Alan Ball chasing the ball is the ultimate advert for sun cream.

Just nine minutes into the game, Carlos Alberto moves towards the halfway line with the ball before hitting a great pass into the stride of Jairzinho, who then beats Terry Cooper to take the ball to the byline before hitting a cross to the back post. And there is Pelé, who powers a header downwards towards the corner at a horrible height for any goalkeeper. But the ‘keeper happens to be Gordon Banks, who somehow gets across from the near post to the far. He doesn’t just palm it out but scoops it over the bar. Enter immortality.

As time progresses, the cult of the Banks save grows. It steadily becomes referred to as the greatest save of all time – as if that is something that anyone is really fit to judge. I personally would argue that Jim Montgomery’s double save against Leeds in the 1973 FA Cup final could give it a run for its money. But the moniker has stuck – aided in England by David Coleman’s commentary of the save being sampled into ‘Three Lions’.

They say a picture tells a thousand words. During the course of football history, there have been many iconic images – Maradona facing five Belgian defenders or Baggio hands on hips after his penalty miss – but one of the most famous is that of Pelé and Bobby Moore embracing at the end of the Brazil-England game. Embracing may be too strong a word given that it involves an Englishman in the 1970s, but there is a definite tenderness in the way Pelé touches Moore’s face while the latter clutches the Brazilian’s discarded shirt proudly in his hand.

It is an image of two legendary players who know that they have just been involved in a titanic struggle. It is an image of pure mutual respect. After all, in a game that, according to the English, had already produced “the greatest save of all time”, it had also, according to the English once again, produced “the greatest tackle of all time” by Moore on Jairzinho. It’s another moment sampled into ‘Three Lions’, ensuring it lives on for generations.

Brazil end up winning all their group games and then proceed to eliminate a useful Peru side in the quarter-finals. Standing between them and a World Cup final are their old foes, Uruguay. It has to be remembered that it was Uruguay who crushed the Brazilian nation by defeating them 2-1 in the 1950 World Cup at the Maracanã. Therefore any big game against Uruguay was always going to cause heightened tension for fans of O Seleção.

The game did not disappoint in that respect with Uruguay taking an early lead. As the half wore on, thoughts must have been flooding back to 1950. Surely Brazil’s greatest side weren’t going to be undone by their tiny neighbours again? But an equaliser just before half-time helped soothe frayed nerves.

With 15 minutes remaining, Brazil finally take the lead through a beautiful Jairzinho goal. A sigh of relief ripples through their fans, but is tempered by the memory that they also led at one stage during the Maracanazo. And so nerves continue to jangle until, with just one minute remaining, Pelé runs at the Uruguayan defence before setting up Rivellino to put the game beyond doubt.

As injury time commences, Brazil look home and dry. As the crowd awaits the final whistle, a through ball from Tostão puts Pelé though onto goal. The goalkeeper, Ladislao Mazurkiewicz, rushes out but it appears that Pelé will get to the ball first. Then it should just be a matter of touching it past the ‘keeper and rolling the ball into the unguarded net for the icing on the cake.

But this is Pelé, a player whose genius almost produced a halfway-line goal earlier in the tournament. To just go around the ‘keeper would be too straightforward. After all, Brazil have won the game. So instead, while running at full speed, Pelé just steps over the ball and lets it run on past a stunned Mazurkiewicz who is stranded in no-man’s land. Quick as you like, Pelé then spins to the right to chase the ball, hits it towards the net, and watches the ball roll agonisingly just wide of the post. It is a move that takes the breath away in a similar fashion to the Cruyff turn in 1974 and is perhaps the greatest goal that never was.

And so Brazil progress to the World Cup final and a date with Italy. The biggest stage in world football. After 18 minutes, Pelé opens the scoring with a header at the far post. But an equaliser by Roberto Boninsegna – he of the Coke can fame – sees the sides level at half-time. Thereafter, goals from Gerson and Jairzinho put Brazil firmly back in the driving seat.As the match approaches the end, Brazilian songs fill the Mexican air.

But there is one more moment of greatness to savour. Brazil retrieve the ball near their own penalty area and start to pass it around with one-touch football. The ball falls to Clodoaldo who almost drunkenly weaves past four Italian players before laying it off to Rivellino, who immediately passes it directly forward to the feet of Jairzinho. He brings the ball across the penalty area and then spots Pelé to his right. A short pass later and O Rei has the ball facing the goal just outside the area with an Italian defender before him.

We’ve all tried it during five-a-side or a Sunday league game – the infamous no-look pass. It is up there with the nutmeg as the ultimate flashy move. With a sixth sense, Pelé just holds the ball momentarily while, behind him, Carlos Alberto is streaking forward on his right-hand side. A heartbeat later and Pelé rolls the ball so, so casually to the right, sensing that Alberto is arriving. And without having to break stride at all, he drills the ball in at full speed. Brazil are world champions once again.

And the final, iconic images of the World Cup are of Brazilian fans rushing onto the field and basically stripping the players of all their kit as souvenirs. Pelé is down to his shorts before being hoisted aloft by fans and paraded around the stadium.

The Brazil team of 1970 was undoubtedly one of the greatest of all, setting a benchmark that has haunted subsequent Seleção sides for generations. And while the whole squad was fantastic, Pelé will always be remembered as the focal point. His four goals, including one in the final, helped push Brazil to victory, just like his goals had 12 years earlier in Sweden. And they were great goals, especially his first against Czechoslovakia.

But Pelé was such an outstanding player that it is more than just his goals that are remembered from 1970. Only Pelé would have the audacity to try to lob the goalkeeper from his own half. Only Pelé would have the nerve to dummy an onrushing ‘keeper and then retrieve the ball and almost score. Only Pelé could power a header so hard and so perfectly into the bottom corner that the resulting save would be described as the greatest save of all time. And only Pelé could finish off the greatest World Cup final team goal with a no-look pass to a colleague.

Pelé was an outstanding goalscorer but also, unlike many other greats in front of goal, so much more. It really wasn’t just about what he did that made him great; it is also the time and place that he did it. That’s what gets results.

#2456. NWSL stats and minutiae after the Quarterfinals

Here’s a look at some stats and minutiae following the National Women’s Soccer League quarterfinals. We’ll keep evolving this space every week to try and keep you informed. Have an idea or an addition? Hit me @thedanlauletta on Bsky or X.

Records referencing teams advancing in the playoffs are reflective of advancing or not even though matches decided on penalty kicks are officially draws.

-Trinity Rodman became the first player in NWSL history to have 2 goals and an assist in a playoff game. There has never been a playoff hat trick.

-Clara Luvanga became the first player in NWSL history to have a goal and 2 assists in a playoff game. There has never been a 3-assist playoff game.

-As the above indicates, Rodman and Luvanga are the first players with 3 combined goals and assists in a playoff game.

-Maddie DiMaria made her NWSL debut for Angel City FC, jumping on for Emily Sams in stoppage time of the second extra time period. She is credited with one minute. DiMaria, fresh off a 12-goal explosion at the U-17 World Cup, is the 2nd player in as many years to debut in a playoff game. Last year was Trinity Byars for the San Diego Wave. Byars had been injured most of the season. DiMaria was signed just ahead of the roster freeze and did not join the team until just ahead of the playoff game.

-Five of the eight ironwomen from the regular season were on playoff teams, and all five played a full 90 minutes over the weekend. Kate Del Fava, Jessie Fleming, Tara Rudd, Kennedy Wesley and keeper Sandy MacIver have now played 2,790 minutes between the regular season and playoffs. Fleming and Wesley’s seasons ended on the weekend.

-Mandy McGlynn joined Adrianna Franch as keepers to win playoff games for more than one club. Sabrina D’Angelo won for the Flash and North Carolina Courage, which the NWSL recognizes as two separate clubs. Franch won for the Flash in 2013, the Portland Thorns in 2017 and 2018 and the Kansas City Current in 2022. McGlynn also won for Gotham FC in 2023.

-Jordyn Bugg has the dubious distinction of being the first player whose Own Goal stood up as a playoff game winner.

-Gotham advanced to the semifinals for the 4th year in a row. Before the start of that streak in 2023 they have never advanced in the playoffs. They did play a semifinal in 2013 when only four teams qualified for the playoffs. They are the 3rd straight defending champion to return to the semifinals. The last two — Gotham in 2024 and the Orlando Pride last year — lost. This will be their 1st time hosting a semifinal.

-The Washington Spirit advanced to the semifinals for the 3rd year in a row and 4th time in 6 years since the playoffs expanded past four teams in 2021. The Spirit advanced directly to the semis three times before that. In 6 prior semifinals, the Spirit are 4-2, having won their last four.

-The Current advanced to the semifinals for the 3rd time including every even year since 2022. They reached the final in 2022.

-The Utah Royals advanced to the semifinal in the club’s first playoff game. They are now the only team to qualify for the playoffs and never concede a playoff goal.

-The Seattle Reign lost in the quarterfinals for the 2nd year in a row. They last advanced in 2023 when they lost the final to Gotham. The Reign missed the playoffs in 2024. In between they lost a semifinal to the Spirit meaning their season has now ended in Washington two years in a row. The Thorns have now been to the playoffs 4 years in a row without reaching the final. That ties the Chicago Red Stars (2015-2018) for the longest such streak in NWSL history. The Red Stars reached the final in 2019 and eventually made the playoffs 7 straight times without winning the title.

-Angel City FC are now 0-2 in the playoffs, both quarterfinals. They were shutout 1-0 both times — in 2023 by the Reign — and are the only team to have participated in the playoffs and not scored a goal. With Sunday’s extra time, that streak covers 210 minutes.

#2455. The Harriers of Norway: welcome to the most unlikely Kidderminster supporters club

On the west coast of Norway, spread across the islands of Hessa, Aspøya, Nørvøya and Uksenøya, at the mouth of the Geirangerfjord, lies Ålesund. It is not a large town, or by in the native Norwegian, but it is a place brimming with appeal. Once razed to the ground at the turn of the 20th century by a devastating fire, it was rebuilt not in wood but stone by the finest Norwegian and German architects of the era.

From its colourful townhouses and their turrets and towers, to its harbourside promenades where the streets shake hands with the sea, Ålesund attracts thousands of visitors a year. Amidst its myriad of paved boulevards, one road in particular is home to a special peculiarity.

At the junction where Kaiser Wilhems Gate meets Harald Torviks Plass, you can find the Brooklyn Bar. With its glass front glimmering, there appears nothing untoward about this New York-themed establishment, but head inside and you can find, tucked away in a not-so-quiet corner festooned in red and white, Norway’s only supporter group dedicated to English National League North side, Kidderminster Harriers.

In order to find out how a town nearly 800 miles from Worcestershire became home to The Harriers of Norway, These Football Times spoke to the group’s founder, Lars Andreas Vegsund. “It started off as a funny thing when our old boys team needed a English club that didn’t have a supporter club in Scandinavia because we wanted to attend the yearly supporter cup in 2019.”

Given the popularity of English football in Norway, the Supporters Cup is an important fixture in the calendar. Organised by Supporterunionen for Britisk Fotball (the Supporters Union of British Football), the knockout tournament takes place every year in Oslo and is contested by the various supporter groups of British football teams. Thousands of players and dozens of fan groups are involved, with the 2022 edition seeing Ipswich take the title for the third occasion.

Lars explains, “We just started going down the different leagues on our phones and looked for a team that would stand out. When my mate called out ‘Kidderminster’, I shouted ‘Harriers’ and that was it. I’d played with the Harriers on different football management games through the years and it just seemed right.”

This Saturday night decision between two mates began as a lonely affair but gathered momentum quickly. By the following week, the pair had found five other Norwegians interested in beginning the Harriers of Norway supporters club and subsequently held their first board meeting in the familiar surrounds of the Brooklyn Bar.

Three years later and the Harriers of Norway can boast 191 members throughout the country in locations as diverse as Bergen, Trondheim, Halden, Mo i Rana and, of course, the capital Oslo. And the common thread unites them all: their affection for an English football club that was last in the Football League in 2005.

But, as Lars is keen to impress, supporting the Harriers is part of a larger agenda. “It has become this rebellion against global football. We enjoy getting back to the roots of English football and getting in touch with proper English football fans, which has been an absolutely mind-blowing experience for us so far. It has surpassed all our expectations.”

As the Harriers of Norway grew in size, so too did they grow in ambition. With Kidderminster struggling to escape the clutches of the National League North, opportunities for their Norwegian fans to watch live matches are scarce. Therefore, they rely primarily on BBC Hereford and Worcestershire radio commentary to catch the 3pm kick-off before later projecting the YouTube highlights onto the basement wall of an old factory within which they have constructed a replica of the terraces of Aggborough Stadium.

Lars proudly shows off photographs of what they have dubbed the “Ålesund Aggborough” and even supplies us with a video. In it, the camera takes you on a tour down a short corridor festooned with Harriers memorabilia before opening out into an area that is a near-identical imitation of the North Stand (save for the welcome addition of well-stocked bar positioned in one corner, of course). Members lean against the red railings, pints in hand, bedecked in replica shirts of years gone by, as they watch an enormous projection of the latest match on the whitewashed wall.

It is more than a worthy substitute, but it doesn’t quite hold the same allure as the real experience – one which many of the club’s members have sampled for themselves over the preceding years. “We have been [to England] four times so far, but it would of course have been more if there hadn’t been any COVID,” says Lars. “We are looking to get back two more times this season [2022/2023]. We really want to get an away game, and were really gutted when the Scarborough match was called off, but hopefully soon we can get on that away game coach.”

As for the club itself, they have been extraordinarily accommodating of their Norwegian fans, even going so far as to arrange a Q&A session with their manager Russell Penn, which he hosted from his own kitchen, no less. Then, during a September 2022 tour, the Norwegian supporters were invited to watch first-team training where club captain Shane Byrne presented them with a kit signed by the entire squad.

And the kindness didn’t stop with the club itself; local supporters took the Norwegians to a cricket match after the postponement of Kidderminster’s weekend fixture following the death of Queen Elizabeth II.

Because of their steadfast devotion to Kiddy, the Harriers of Norway have been the subject of a TV special by Norwegian broadcaster Viaplay, who travelled to Norway’s west coast to witness the Ålesund Aggborough and interview several supporters, with their segment airing ahead of the third round FA cup tie against West Ham – the Harriers’ most high-profile match since their cup run of 2013/14 which culminated in a 1-0 fourth-round loss to Sunderland at the Stadium of Light.

But when it comes to a hypothetical fixture between Kiddy and his local Norwegian club, Lars is in no doubt as to where his loyalties lie. “Without a doubt, the Harriers. No question. This club and their fans have shown us the true meaning of support and brought us back to our childhood feelings of supporting our ‘own’ team. It has truly been an absolutely amazing experience so far, and I can`t wait to see how far this will take us all.”

Perhaps one day, they will get to witness their beloved English club in the Football League once more, evoking memories of yesteryear when the deep pockets of retail magnate Lionel Newton finally lifted Kidderminster out of non-league for the first time in their history.

The Harriers had won the Conference before in 1993/94 but had been denied entry to Division Three because of stringent fire safety laws implemented in the wake of the fire at Valley Parade that had claimed 56 lives. At the time, Aggborough’s main stand was constructed mostly out of timber, and despite the construction of a new cantilever stand in time for the new season, the Football League rejected the club’s application.

Kidderminster eventually achieved promotion, winning the Conference by nine points in 1999/2000, whereupon they embarked on a four-year stay in the Football League. These were the halcyon days of the Danes, when Jan Mølby held court in Aggborough, ably assisted by star striker “Bomber” Bo Henriksen along with winger Thomas Skovbjerg.

It is a fact not lost on the Scandinavian admirers of today. “I think there has been three playing Danes,” Lars says. “But to have a Norwegian play for Harriers would be a dream come true for us. We can definitely be Harriers’ eyes and ears here in Norway if the right talent shows up!”

As of writing, Kidderminster have no Scandinavians, let alone Norwegians, on their books, and are firmly ensconced in the middle order of the National League North, with promotion or relegation seemingly as unlikely as the other. Despite this, that won’t stop the Harriers of Norway from filling the stands of the Ålesund Aggborough each weekend or taking the short flight across the North Sea to the West Midlands when the opportunity arises.

And who knows, maybe one day Kidderminster Harriers won’t just find success on the pitches of the National League but on the artificial turf in Oslo’s Supporters Cup, too.

By Josh Butler @joshisbutler90 Photo: Express & Star

#2454. La situation se corse pour les U19

Mal en point(s) les U19 Stéphanois (7 points en 9 rencontres) se déplaçaient en Corse ce matin pour y affronter Bastia, 3 points de plus au compteur. Un peu rassurés après les promesses entrevues face à Monaco (1-2), les protégés de Frédéric Dugand ont à nouveau affiché leurs limites, s'inclinant à nouveau (c'est la 4ème fois) sur le score de 0-3 !

En première période, la possession est verte, mais de façon stérile. Les Stéphanois sont maladroits et rejoignent la mi-temps sans le moindre tir cadré ! En face, Bastia va de son côté être très réaliste et  tromper à 2 reprises, sur autant d’occasions, le portier vert Lorik Vial, aux 40ème et 44ème minutes. (Bastia 2  ASSE 0 ; mi-temps).

En seconde période les Verts ne sont pas plus inspirés, avec une seule occasion, une tentative de Fousseny Sidibé Kaloga bien stoppé par le gardien Bastiais. La fin de match tourne au cauchemar, avec un rouge récolté par ce même Fousseny Kaloga et un troisième pion encaissé sur la 3ème tentative corse (90ème) ! (Bastia 3  ASSE 0 ; score final).

Avec cette 5ème défaite consécutive (la 7ème au total), les jeunes Verts sont dorénavant avant derniers et relégables, seul Borgo (1 point) faisant moins bien qu’eux. Une réaction est attendue et obligatoire la semaine prchaine, avec la réception de l'US Cap d'Ail, 12 points, auteur d'un nul aujourd'hui face à Balma (2-2).

La Composition : Vial – Akil (Demassieux 70ème), E.Mnemoi, Assoumani (Lengi 46ème), Jolivet, Marliac, N.Mouton, O.Mendy, Kaloga, Zibi, Vibert (Gobé 62ème).

La réaction de Frédéric Dugand : « Il nous a manqué de tout. De la justesse technique, de la justesse dans nos choix défensifs comme offensifs. On ne peut pas rivaliser si on ne montre pas plus de caractère pour défendre et plus de lucidité devant le but. On a eu la possession mais quand tu ne cadres pas un tir..Notre production est insuffisante et la situation devient préoccupante »

#2453. Access, Not Chances: How Como Took Manchester United Apart – LC

von Next Generation am 24.10.2026 in den Kategorien Champions League,Uncategorized mit 0 Kommentaren

Como beat Manchester United 4-1 — and in this case the scoreline really is a fair expression of the game. For long stretches the match was one-sided, not in terms of chance volume but in terms of access: Como dictated in every phase where the ball went, who received it, and under what conditions it had to be played on. United never got on terms in any of those phases.

Cesc Fàbregas’s side showed two things that rarely go together. Out of possession, a pressing structure with clear direction, isolation of one side, and man-marking that applied near the ball only for the action in progress while everything around it was already speculating on the second ball. And in possession, a positional game of remarkable technical maturity that ties opponents in, switches play, and works systematically into the space behind them. The 4-1 is therefore less an outlier than evidence of work that has been built up over recent seasons.

This analysis goes through the phases one by one: first Como in possession and United’s response, then the work against the ball from the high press to defending the box, and finally the goals.

In build-up, Como moved away from their nominal 4-2-3-1 and sat closer to a 4-3-3, with the eights as the real variable: very free in their movement and above all active in the half-spaces. The base structure stayed stable — a flat four plus a six in front of them, sometimes ahead of the line, sometimes slightly behind the forward line.

Close to their own goal, Como consistently involved goalkeeper Butez as an additional central player in the build-up. That created a five-against-four against United’s front line — awkward on paper, more awkward still in execution, because Como didn’t use the overload to play through but to tie opponents in. From there, the same shape kept appearing on both the right and the left: centre-back, full-back, a player from the half-position in the eight space, and a six alongside. A diamond that wasn’t an end in itself but had a purpose: the diagonal route out.

Como’s build-up structure. From a 4-1 (flat four), the half-positions with Paz and Perrone are added. Small triangles and diamonds emerge. The three attackers ahead of them create additional options in behind.

One detail deserves particular attention. At times the full-backs stood not wide but flat, in a half-position. That sounds like a nuance, but it had a clear function: it vacated the wing and created the space the eights could drop into — Paz and Perrone did so regularly. If you don’t occupy the wing yourself, you force the opponent to guard it anyway.

ManU got no access near the ball and left large diagonal spaces open on the far side.

For United’s midfielders this was close to unsolvable. Tielemans, Mount and Andrey Santos spent the whole game struggling to establish any responsibility at all, let alone get into duels. When an eight dropped out, they couldn’t follow, and if one of them was tied in by it, a two-against-one opened up on the far wing. Como didn’t create that situation once; they created it serially.

The decisive mechanism lay in receiving and relaying the ball. The player in the deeper position usually worked with two touches: the first took the ball backwards, the second relayed it to the free teammate. At the end of every one of those actions stood a player with the game in front of him — and from that open position he could switch play.

What made it possible were the preparatory movements. Paz and captain Da Cunha first lured their markers in the wrong direction and then worked with the head start they’d bought. That head start isn’t only space, it’s above all time: time to control the ball first and relay it second, rather than having to do both in one touch.

A scene in the 17th minute is typical. Mason Mount steps out, Mazraoui goes into the duel at the same time — nominally United are in an overload here. Only neither of them really gets to the opponent, because both are too late. Paz can therefore calmly take his touch backwards and switch play directly with the second, dissolving the pressure before it had even formed.

When the build-up ran down the right, it showed in a recurring pattern: Paz and Da Cunha took the first touch backwards or inside and then switched with the left foot out of a closed body position. The players they found were systematically in open positions — Milla, the far-side six, or the wing-to-wing connection directly.

In the second half, Como adjusted the shape and more often played with two sixes, to form the diamonds faster and switch to the far-side six faster. Couto stood out in this: the right-back repeatedly played the chip into the six or ten space — six or seven times in a row during one spell. It was mainly Paz who received the ball there and could launch the attack.

In the second half Como focus on those diagonal spaces and look for them mainly with chipped balls.

Especially striking inside the diamond are the rotations between the players. Because of the connections between them, they moved in rotation depending on running path, space and ball movement. The same recurring spaces were re-occupied. Under pressure on the ball carrier, the outer players pushed flat or ran in behind the opponents; the highest player in the diamond burst out of the cover shadow and became the reference point in depth. On a deep pass, the two wide players released and joined the depth, able to offer themselves again immediately in an open body position. If the pass went via the flat wide players, the spaces in front of the new ball carrier could be run into. Every rotation, every positional adjustment was coordinated with the others and, in the end, produced a stream of pressure-resolving passes while Manchester United chased the press in vain.

Como bridged the middle third exceptionally quickly, via dribbles at speed and diagonal passes. Behind it stood a recognisable principle: first tie the opponent to one wing, then get behind them via the diagonal, and in the final third do the same thing again. In sum, that produced the shape of a Z — build-up on the right, transition on the left, finish from the right again.

In this example Como pin ManU in the press with their short passing. Thanks to the extra attacker on the ball-near side they can play through the pressure and switch.

The connections between wingers and striker carried these attacks and were deliberately kept flexible. The wide players sometimes stayed wide, sometimes came short, sometimes tucked inside. Douvikas accordingly either waited deep in front of the line for the chipped ball or, when space opened up on the wing, received the deeper pass and then ran in behind along the wing as soon as the ball sat on the full-back’s open foot. That flexibility produced the overloads on one side, and the overloads produced the central overload.

In the final third one element was added that is rare in fast transition teams: patience. Como drew opponents towards them with dribbles and short passes, used back-passes when needed, and then switched in front of the block. Da Cunha, Baturina and Paz were the three who could tie opponents in and then find the diagonal. They created the positions on the diagonal, were available to receive, and used their space to apply pressure. The block was usually tied in with short touches, the switch and the position behind the opponent prepared, and quick finishes sought.

The intensity in possession shouldn’t be underestimated. Practically every attack involved at least three or four players, the width was occupied, the centre likewise, and there were multiple options throughout. What they looked for almost every time was the space behind the opponent on the far side — exactly the zone that is closed last when a block shifts across.

Paz brought the right profile for this pattern. A strong left foot cutting inside from the right, he repeatedly dropped into the right-hand blind side of his opponents, got shots away there with few touches, and racked up the most shots of the match. That the finishes generally came off few touches isn’t a detail but the consequence of the time won further back.

As the move continues, Como again look for the blind side of the defenders. Here Douvikas and Paz are positioned in behind, with Da Cunha joining in front of the back line. After briefly pinning the opponents, the switch reaches Da Cunha, who misses the target from distance.

What carries all of this is the technical execution. Soft passes, sharp ones when the moment called for it, consistently well timed and played into the right foot — for ninety minutes. Passing that secure at that tempo is what makes a variable concept actually retrievable.

United’s basic problem out of possession was the hybrid. They pressed half man-oriented, but with a plus-one in the last line — a construction that forces compromises in both directions. It demands access up front that it doesn’t fund at the back.

There were certainly moments when it worked. When Dalot pushed through into the press on the right and passed his man backwards, a clean man-orientation emerged all the way up to the front — and with it a clear assignment for Mount, out of which the ball could be won. But that stayed the exception. Most of the time Dalot sat too flat out of possession, so United couldn’t trigger the duels up front and went into the press a man short.

Mount was the most conspicuous case in this respect. He barely got into a duel across the whole match because the decision to step out always came too late. Against a team that works with preparatory movements, a late decision is practically the same as none: the opponent already has the head start before the journey even begins.

On top of that came a problem on the far side. There, United’s winger frequently failed to protect the depth — usually Mbeumo, who jogged back rather than closing the space. But that was precisely the target zone of Como’s diagonal switches. It allowed them to change sides almost at will and regularly find an open structure on the other side.

The second half brought no improvement. The distances to opponents stayed large, and centrally what was actually intended still didn’t materialise. Michael Carrick’s double change at half-time was meant to bring more physicality to the six with Carlos Baleba, but it didn’t solve the problem — the assignments still didn’t work, the duels in the centre still didn’t happen, and the wide positions dragged the eights out further, which opened new spaces.

In the end the energy simply wasn’t there to press with the necessary intensity. United’s press became increasingly static, and a static press against an opponent with this passing quality yields not a single ball win — it only hands them the starting positions they’re looking for anyway.

Como started the game in a high press and sustained it above all in the first half, with isolated spells after the break too. It was triggered on back-passes and goal kicks — and, remarkably, by their own goals: after every strike the team immediately pushed high again instead of managing the lead in a deeper block.

The steering ran consistently towards United’s left build-up side. The reason is personnel: Harry Maguire played there with his weaker left foot as the outside foot, and next to him stood another right-footer in Noussair Mazraoui on the left. Two right-footers on one build-up side means the ball always has to be taken back inside to play on — exactly where Como were closing the door. The press was usually triggered by the left-sided forward, with the ball ending up at either Maguire or Mazraoui.

Pressing structure after the change in the second half.

In the centre Como defended man-oriented, with both sixes pushing very high and taking flat passes into United’s midfielders out of the game. That removed the short route through the middle as an option and left the long ball. But the long ball triggered nothing for United: the second balls went to Como practically every time.

That isn’t chance, it’s running work. The sixes consistently tracked the negative pressing paths back, anticipated the long ball early, and were in front of the line before it arrived. Luis Milla covered the most ground of any player on the pitch in this pattern — recovery runs after being played past, doubling up on the ball, attacking the second ball. When the long ball came from Maguire or one of the full-backs, a six was regularly in front of the line with an intense sprint, sealing the centre, taking away the diagonal follow-up passes and attacking the loose balls.

Defending the long ball and extra support on the second ball.

Once the ball was on one side, that side was isolated. The near-side forward had access to the centre-back and dropped back a touch when the pass went to the full-back, so that he covered centre-back and six simultaneously and closed the square pass. The far-side forward marked the goalkeeper. That served two functions at once: it took away United’s escape route via the keeper along with the switch, and it kept a player in position for the moment of the turnover.

The double pivot worked in a deliberate half-position. The near-side six stayed tight to his man, the far-side one dropped slightly behind him — securing the space and at the same time establishing access to the far-side centre-back in United’s back three.

The last line defended largely man-for-man in the high press, and very tightly. But the decisive detail is the one that carries the whole concept: the man-marking near the ball applied only to the action in progress. Around it, players were already releasing from their assignments and orienting towards the second ball. That is only retrievable at very high intensity — and it’s the reason United’s forced long balls produced not a single usable moment.

When Como dropped a line, the man-orientation at the second height stayed exceptionally high. Here too the back-pass served as the trigger to push up as a unit and tip back into man-marking. If United were in a closed body position, the Comaschi had already pushed up far enough to attack the back-pass at the moment it was played — a pattern that led directly to the 3-0. The half-position was at work there again: closing down level with the centre-back while simultaneously prepared to push through onto the next player deeper.

In the first half Como still had problems assigning the half-positions against ManU’s 3-2-5. In this example Fernandes moves to the wing, Como fail to establish responsibility and access and are played through at mid-height.

Up to half-time, though, Como had a structural problem with this. The pure man-marking didn’t come off cleanly, because of the two sixes in front of the line, one should really have tucked in and taken over the half-position for the centre-backs. That didn’t happen consistently. The consequence: a centre-back stepped out, the space behind him stayed unoccupied, and that was exactly what United kept attacking.

The pattern of pressing onto Manchester United’s left side continued in the second half, now with Dalot at full-back. The press was still triggered by Douvikas, with the ball-near winger pushing up as a second striker to press the centre-back. Paz focused on the visitors’ ball-near six and Couto pushed through onto Dalot. Through the central connections the game was isolated on one side.

At half-time Como adjusted. One six moved directly into the line, with the far-side winger pushing in onto the six — they now pressed out of a 5-2-1-2. Lucas Da Cunha pressed through from the right onto Maguire, while Nico Paz picked up United’s six. The central forward pressed the central centre-back and from there carried on to the goalkeeper. The far-side wide midfielder and the remaining six were poised — one onto United’s free six, one onto the far-side centre-back — again in that half-position between opponent and the space to be protected.

ManU building up high against the man-oriented Italians.

The effect was immediately visible. Como controlled the half-positions, got access right into the last line throughout, and set the rhythm of the match from then on. The adjustment solved exactly the problem the first half had left open, without changing the underlying principle.

In the final phase Como defended from a very deep line inside the box. That left barely any space behind the line to play into — which United hardly looked for anyway. The visitors attacked little depth and rarely occupied the width in the final third, so Como could stay compact without being punished for it.

Accordingly, a lot of players stood very centrally in and in front of the box. That produced numerous cover shadows and a numerical superiority around the ball, which allowed them to steer actively within the block rather than merely react. At times they deliberately steered inside, to guide the opponent into the prepared congestion and cover from a deeper position.

Deep back line in the box, centre closed and play steered inside. The box defending allowed the English side shots from distance.

The crucial point is that Como left the gaps open not despite this set-up but because of it. If you pack the box and secure the depth, you give up the space in front of the line — and that is exactly where United were supposed to shoot from.

The numbers vindicate the decision. Taking the conceded goal out of the box, Como allowed nine shots from outside the penalty area across ninety minutes, worth roughly 0.24 xG combined; only three of them were even on target. On top of that, of the four shots inside the box, two came from at least 14 to 15 metres and effectively belong in the long-range category as well. United accepted the invitation, and the shooting quality was perfectly decent — it’s just that with that scoring probability over a whole match, the most likely outcome is precisely what happened.

1-0, Nico Paz (2′) — The goal comes before United are even set. Como take the goal kick quickly and play straight to the full-back, luring the visitors into the press — only not cleanly. Mason Mount triggers the pressure and is played past, and on the second ball he goes into the duel as well instead of holding the middle and looking for the space where he could pick the ball up. That is exactly what opens the centre, the space for the second ball is there, and Paz can play it through.

What follows is the transition principle in its purest form: a quick switch to the diagonal side, then short passes against a very deep line. Matheus Cunha doesn’t pick up the player behind him and leaves the ten space open, where Paz is standing. He needs two touches because neither Cunha from above nor Maguire from his distance gets into the duel. Lammens, for his part, doesn’t defend the goal with his cover shadow but takes the near post — which leaves the far corner to a strong left foot. The curled finish into it is quality, though.

2-0, Anastasios Douvikas (49′, assist Paz) — Same zone, same cause. Bryan Mbeumo doesn’t choose to shut the centre but closes the centre-back, which creates the space for Da Cunha, who drives forward and plays Martin Baturina in. Centrally, Mount again fails to pick up his man. Out wide, Amad Diallo, introduced at half-time, generates no pressure centrally, so Mazraoui can’t take over the deep wide player in the first place.

The result is Paz behind the opponent, in the ten space, dribbling unopposed at goal. Matthijs de Ligt establishes no reference to Douvikas’s run in behind and slips as well — a one-against-one with the goalkeeper that Douvikas finishes coolly.

3-0, Nico Paz (57′) — The only goal that comes directly out of the work against the ball. Como are in the midfield press in a closed position with access to the inside lane, win the ball there and punish a lapse of concentration in the visitors’ build-up. At the end, Paz is alone in front of Lammens again.

4-0, Jacobo Ramón (76′, assist Kaiki) — This goal comes from a longer possession spell and shows the assignment problem in its clearest form. Mazraoui is too narrow and has no access to the wide player. Diallo stands in the space with access to neither the central player nor the full-back nor the winger — an orientation that doesn’t work in any direction.

Como switch to Máximo Perrone, who can slide the ball out wide because the space is simply free. From there comes the cross from an open body position, and in the centre Como run a two-against-one at the end of which Ramón scores.

4-1, Joshua Zirkzee (90′) — Como’s only lapse, and one in a phase in which the team had already dropped very deep. United get the ball to the wing, it’s two against two in the box, and the cross is initially only feinted. Zirkzee orients himself well forwards at that moment, while Como’s defenders are already stepping out after the feinted cross. Diallo’s ball in behind the line is strong, the offside call is razor-thin in his favour, and Zirkzee takes two touches before finishing one-against-one with the goalkeeper. A blemish, not a structural problem.

The common denominator — Three of Como’s four goals come in the same zone: the space in front of and behind United’s line that nobody takes responsibility for. Mount is involved in two of those scenes through an assignment he never establishes, Diallo in two more after coming on. Nico Paz is at the heart of three of the four goals, twice as scorer, once as the provider — always out of the opponent’s blind side.

Como’s 4-1 has one common cause across every phase, and it lies less in any single idea than in its execution under continuous load. Out of possession they steered, isolated and speculated on the second ball — with man-marking that applied near the ball only for the action in progress and was already dissolved around it. In possession they tied opponents in, switched play and worked systematically into the space behind. Both require eleven players to anticipate a teammate’s decision, and both functioned over the full distance.

The connecting detail is the half-position. In the press, the far-side six stood between opponent and the space to be protected; in possession, the eights worked out of the same zone, and the full-backs occupied it flat in order to vacate the wing for exactly those players. Como, in other words, occupied the position in both directions from which two jobs can be done at once — which is why the side could neither be played past in the press nor be pinned in the build-up.

For United the diagnosis is more uncomfortable than the result. The problem wasn’t individual errors but that the team never, in any phase, got into the duels it needed. The mixture of half man-orientation and a plus-one in the last line funded no access up front, and without access every decision is made too late — from Mount in the centre to Mbeumo failing to secure the far-side depth. Carrick’s double change at half-time was meant to bring physicality to the six with Carlos Baleba, but it changed nothing about the assignments, and in Diallo a player came on wide who reached neither one opponent nor the other in his space. That the energy ran out in the end was a consequence rather than a cause.

That leaves the context. A 4-1 against Manchester United is no proof in itself, and Como’s finishing was exceptionally efficient on the night. What showed regardless of the result, though, is a team with a recognisable, rehearsed answer in all four phases of the game — and one that put a technical maturity on the pitch in possession that you wouldn’t readily credit to a side promoted two years ago.
